| new: cfuture (context future) | "a local future which cannot be passed outside the function without being touched". It is implemented with the CFUT hardware tag, "using much less overhead than cboxes in CONCURRENTSMALLTALK". | pp. 8, 11, 178 |
| new: distributed object | "an object that can process many methods at the same time without any serialization bottlenecks other than those required by the algorithm". The OS routes group-name messages to constituents. | pp. 2, 20 |
| new: home node and object migration | Each object has a home node, which tracks its location; migration uses RequestObject, MigrateObject, UpdateHome and Unlock messages. | pp. 68–72 |
| new: criticality | A number limiting what a system call may do (e.g. "No message sends"). It was introduced because "almost all of its routines are non-reentrant". | p. 58 |
| new: reduction of method calls to function calls | A compiler optimisation that removes method dispatch and often inlines the call, "highly successful". | pp. 4, 49 |
| new: tail forwarding | A tail-forwarded call is "one call and no return", about 36 instructions against about 100. | pp. 104, 106 |
| new: parallelism control | "a parallel computer can fail if a program exhibiting too much parallelism is run on it". A queue-threshold switch to sequential evaluation was explored. | pp. 121–124 |
| new: fanout bottleneck | Serialising copies of immutable objects through their single home node. | p. 119 |

## Notes
- **Source read:** a scan of MIT AI Lab TR AITR-1321, the second edition (updated September 26, 1991) of the May 1989 S.M. thesis. Downloaded from DSpace@MIT (hdl 1721.1/7090) through the bitstream API and saved as `papers/P70.pdf` (246 PDF pages, image-only, no text layer). The DTIC copy (ADA259417) returned HTTP 403. The 1991 edition does not include "the newest changes" (hardware I/O, debugging aids, first-silicon workarounds) (p. 1).
- **Coverage (pass 2):** read in full: front matter, Ch. 1–2, Ch. 3 (pp. 22, 45–50), Ch. 4 (pp. 51–80, 84), Ch. 5 (p. 85), Ch. 6–9, Appendix A.1 (pp. 129–130), Appendix D (pp. 176–183). Not read: most of Ch. 3 (pp. 23–44), pp. 81–83 and 86–97, Appendices A.2–A.15, B, C and F, and the bibliography.
- **Criterion:** the screening proposal of I1 is confirmed by I1(a) (SEND/SUSPEND instructions, p. 183), I1(b) (hardware queues and dispatch, p. 179) and I1(c) (Cosmos inter-node services are message protocols, pp. 70–76). The full text may also meet I2: Ch. 7 evaluates performance on an architecture its author calls "message-driven" (p. 176), with simulated measurements and stated causes (pp. 101–114). I2 does not require silicon. No exclusion criterion found. X5: a university technical report and master's thesis. X8: this is not the same system and results as P71 (the 1988 Optimist compiler report) or P12; the overlap with P12 is limited to describing COSMOS and CST.
- **Hardware–language content (relevant to SQ9; the field is n/a under I1):** the author argues that MDP tags let the compiler skip type analysis at little cost (p. 11). He proposes ISA changes (MOVE from ID registers to memory, a corrected FIP after faults, larger queues and XLATE tables; for the shortage of tags, several XLATE tables or multi-word keys) and hardware register shadowing for fast context switches (p. 125). He also lists four ways to add floating point, from software emulation through fault handlers to an on-chip FPU or RAP chips (pp. 117–118).
- **Measurement basis:** every number in Ch. 7 comes from MDPSim (simulated) or from instruction counts (analytical), not from J-Machine silicon (pp. 102, 108). MDPSim "assumes that the MDPs are connected by crossbar network" (p. 121).
- **Criteria (gate 3c, 2026-10-12):** I1 and I2. The I2-only fields (*Hardware–language trade-off*, *Adoption factors*) are filled in the follow-up pass with the SQ files.

# Selection criteria

A paper is included if it meets at least one inclusion criterion and no exclusion criterion. Each verdict names the criterion that decided it. There is no restriction on publication date. "Message-based" in these criteria means: meets I1.

Terms used in the criteria and the SQs:
- **Below the programming language:** in the operating system kernel, the instruction set, microcode or hardware; not in a language runtime, library or virtual machine hosted on a conventional kernel (as in X2).
- **Written in its own objects and messages:** the level's code is objects receiving messages in the system's own model, not a lower language, microcode or hardware outside that model.
- **Without changing either:** neither the sender's nor the receiver's code, nor how they name each other, is modified to place the component between them.

# P102

## Reference
David Wentzlaff, Anant Agarwal (2009). *Factored Operating Systems (fos): The Case for a Scalable Operating System for Multicores*. ACM SIGOPS Operating Systems Review 43(2), pp. 76–85. https://doi.org/10.1145/1531793.1531805

## Deepest pass
2

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** A position and design paper with motivating measurements. It argues that SMP operating systems cannot scale to "1000+ core systems" (p. 2), measures two Linux scaling problems (p. 3–4), and describes the design of a new message-passing OS (fos) whose prototype is "under active development" (p. 2, p. 8). fos itself is not evaluated.
- **Context:** Microkernels (Mach, L3, L4; p. 2, p. 8), scalable shared-memory kernels (Tornado/K42, Hive, Disco/Cellular Disco, Corey; p. 9), distributed OSes (Amoeba, Sprite, Clouds; p. 9) and distributed Internet services (DNS, BitTorrent, Chord, AFS, GFS; p. 9–10). The authors' own Raw and Tilera on-chip networks are cited for message costs (p. 8).
- **Correctness:** The Linux measurements are on real hardware (p. 3), and the cache study runs in a QEMU-based simulator (p. 4). The case for fos rests on argument, for example "We believe that the shared nothing, message passing only, approach will encourage OS developers to think very carefully about exactly what data is being shared, which will lead to more scalability" (p. 5). The paper names its own open questions in Section 3.4 (p. 8).
- **Contributions:** (1) A measurement showing that the Linux 2.6.24.7 physical page allocator "does not scale beyond 8 cores under heavy load" (p. 2, Fig. 1 p. 3). (2) A simulated measurement of OS/application cache interference on Apache2 (p. 4). (3) Three recommendations: avoid hardware locks, separate OS from application cores, and avoid global cache-coherent shared memory (p. 5). (4) The fos design: a microkernel with mailbox messaging, OS services split into fleets of servers bound to cores, a name server, and space multiplexing instead of time multiplexing (p. 5–7).
- **Clarity:** Well structured and readable. The figure labels in the author PDF use an odd font encoding (the text cannot be extracted), but the rendered figures are legible. The message format is not described.

## Quality
| Q | Answer | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | yes | The abstract and introduction say so in one place: "This work investigates why simply scaling up traditional symmetric multiprocessor operating systems is not sufficient ... and proposes how to build a factored operating system (fos)" (p. 1). |
| Q2 | partly | Receiver naming (symbolic mailbox names, name cache, name server; p. 6), delivery ("reliable messaging layer", p. 6) and busy receiver ("If a receive mailbox is full, the sending client send call returns an error", p. 6) are described. Message format and ordering are not. |
| Q3 | no | The claims about fos rest on design and argument. The prototype is only said to boot (p. 8). The Linux studies used to motivate it are measured on hardware (p. 3) and simulated (p. 4), but they do not evaluate fos. |
| Q4 | partly | The Linux allocator scaling is judged against a hypothetical baseline ("perfect scaling would be bars all the same height", p. 3). The fos claims against Mach, L4 and K42 (p. 8–9) are not measured. |
| Q5 | partly | Workloads and hardware or simulator configurations are given (p. 3, p. 4), and the allocator workload is partly justified (p. 4). The number of runs is not reported. |
| Q6 | yes | The only quantitative claims in the abstract and conclusion are core-count projections ("100's to 1,000's of cores", "double every 18 months"). Body text repeats them as the authors' own extrapolation, with no citation of their own. Only the transistor trend behind them is cited: "The ITRS road-map[1] and the continuation of Moore's Law[16] forecast exponential increases in the number of transistors" (p. 1–2). |
| Q7 | partly | Lock contention is isolated by an oprofile breakdown by function (Fig. 1, p. 3). Interference misses are isolated by simulating separate OS-only and application-only caches (p. 4). The architectural overhead is only "believed to be caused by contention in the hardware memory system" (p. 3). The causes of fos's expected benefits are asserted only (p. 7–9). |
| Q8 | yes | Section 3.4 *Challenges* (p. 8) is dedicated to open questions and costs, such as core-to-core latency, shared structures like the buffer cache, lock servers, and multi-sequence operations. |
| Q9 | no | Both authors design fos (p. 1–2), and the paper does not evaluate fos. The Linux systems measured are third-party, but they are only motivating baselines. |

## Extracted fields
| Field | Value | Page |
|---|---|---|
| Reference | Wentzlaff & Agarwal (2009), ACM SIGOPS OSR 43(2): 76–85 (range from Crossref). P102. Included under I1 (I1(c): kernel services communicate by messages). Version read: the author preprint, marked "To appear in ACM SIGOPS Operating System Review ... April 2009", 11 PDF pages with no page numbers printed. Pages below are PDF pages of `papers/P102.pdf`. The publisher's layout was not seen, so no offset is established (75 is likely (inferred), not verified). | p. 1 |
| Paper type | Position or analytical argument (p. 1–2, p. 5); design (fos, p. 5–7); evaluation of a third-party system (Linux scaling and cache studies, p. 3–4); implementation status only, not described in detail (p. 8) | p. 1–8 |
| System | **fos** (factored operating system). Built at MIT CSAIL by Wentzlaff and Agarwal (p. 1); Charles Gruenwald thanked "for help on fos" (p. 10). Year: under development at writing, 2009 (inferred from the venue date). Status: running kernel, partial prototype: "fos is currently booting on 16 core x86_64 hardware and a QEMU simulation of up to 255 processors ... currently consists of a bootloader, microkernel, messaging layer with capability checking, and name server. We are beginning to implement OS Layer servers." **Linux 2.6.24.7** and **Linux 2.6.18.8** (third-party, deployed) are measured as motivating cases (p. 3, p. 4). | p. 1, 3, 4, 8, 10 |
| Levels with message semantics | **Hardware:** not stated for fos in general. fos "does not require architectures to support intra-machine shared memory" (p. 9). On the x86_64 prototype, no (inferred): the paper says "shared memory is the only means by which a desktop hardware architecture allows core-to-core communication" (p. 4), and messages travel "via on-chip networks or shared memory" (p. 6). **Microcode:** not stated. **Instruction set:** not stated. **Kernel, between cores:** partly. "Servers communicate only via the messaging interface provided by the microkernel layer" and "The OS layer does not internally utilize shared memory" (p. 6). The microkernel and its delegated name and privilege servers "communicate via microkernel messaging" (p. 7). Message-only operations: application-to-OS-service requests, server-to-server and fleet traffic, and microkernel-to-delegated-service traffic (p. 6–7). Other paths: applications may share memory between their own cores "if the underlying hardware supports it" (p. 6), and the message transport itself may use shared memory (p. 6). **Kernel, within a core:** partly. System calls are turned into messages: "A small translation library is used to turn system calls into messages from application to an OS layer server" (p. 6). The send itself is a call into the local microkernel ("The message proxy library calls the fos-microkernel to send the message", p. 6). Traps and interrupts: not stated. **Runtime:** a message proxy library on the application side (p. 6). **Language:** not stated. **Started message-based and later added other paths:** not stated (design-stage paper). | p. 4, 6, 7, 9 |
| Receiving unit and state ownership | The unit is a receive mailbox owned by a "fos client", which is "The code executing on a single core under the fos-microkernel" (p. 6). Each client "can allocate a large number of receive mailboxes" (p. 6). A server is "bound to a core" (p. 5) and "executes solely on a dedicated processor core" (p. 6). State: OS-layer servers do not share memory: "the servers which provide the file system and the virtual memory management do not share memory with each other" (p. 8). Mailbox buffers "live in the receiving client's address space" (p. 8), so the microkernel writes into them (inferred: "The receive microkernel deposits message in the file system server's request mailbox", p. 6). Applications may share memory among their own cores (p. 6). | p. 5, 6, 8 |
| Message mechanism | **Sync/async:** asynchronous. "send routines and receive routines do not need to be synchronized like in the L4 operating system ... The use of large input mailboxes decouples send and receive synchronization" (p. 8). **Naming:** "Clients can attach symbolic names to their receive mailboxes and publish these names"; "fos clients send messages to named mailboxes" (p. 6). The microkernel keeps a name cache and delegates lookups to the name server fleet, which "maintains the canonical mailbox name to physical core and mailbox directory" (p. 6). Names can map one-to-many, with the server instance chosen "based off of physical proximity or load balancing" (p. 6). Namespace "can be protected" (p. 6), and the messaging layer has "capability checking" (p. 8). **Delivery:** "reliable transport and enqueuing" (p. 6); "on-chip communications are considered to be reliable" (p. 6). **Ordering:** not stated. **Buffering:** "large buffers which live in the receiving client's address space" (p. 8). **Busy receiver:** "If a receive mailbox is full, the sending client send call returns an error" (p. 6). **Dispatch:** a server has two inbound mailboxes, one for new requests and one for responses, and "prioritizes responses over requests". It is cooperative and non-preemptive; a long-latency operation stores a continuation, and processing yields to the next transaction (p. 7, Fig. 6). Most servers use "stateless protocols" (p. 7). | p. 6, 7, 8 |
| Non-message primitives | (1) **Application shared memory** at the application level, "if the underlying hardware supports it". Reason: "While coherent shared memory may be inherently unscalable in the large, in a small application, it can be quite useful" (p. 6). (2) **Shared memory as message transport** in the microkernel: "transport the message ... via on-chip networks or shared memory". Reason: not stated (p. 6). (3) **Microkernel name cache** and **read-only privilege cache** inside the microkernel. Reason: "fast name lookups and a large namespace at the same time" (p. 6); privileges cached "in a read only manner" (p. 7). (4) **Static privileges** given to privilege-manager servers by the microkernel, "so that a privilege fixed point can be reached" (p. 7). (5) **Fixed knowledge of physical location** of delegated services in the microkernel, "In order to prevent dependency cycles" (p. 7). (6) **Hardware locking instructions:** not used: "if a lock is absolutely necessary, hardware locking instructions are not used as servers are not preempted" (p. 7). Interrupts, direct memory access, I/O ports: not stated. | p. 6, 7 |
| Self-definition | OS services (naming, privilege, memory allocation, file system, scheduling) are written as servers communicating by microkernel messages (p. 6–7). The microkernel is outside that model. It "is platform dependent, provides protection mechanisms but not protection policy, and implements a fast machine-dependent communication infrastructure" (p. 2), and "controls access to resources (protection), provides a communication API and code spawning API ... and maintains a name cache" (p. 5). Implementation language: not stated. Whether a running program can inspect or change these levels: not stated. Cost of the base: not stated. | p. 2, 5, 6, 7 |
| Interposition | Not stated as such. The name server "allows for redirection of mailboxes if a client changes physical location" and "provides a one-to-many mapping function" (p. 6), which may allow a component to be placed behind a published name without changing the sender (inferred). The translation library sits between the application's system-call interface and OS servers (p. 6). Cost: not stated. | p. 6 |
| Operating system functions | **Protection:** microkernel mechanisms plus a privilege service "implemented as a fleet of servers in the OS layer", cached in the microkernel and invalidated by message (p. 7); namespace protection (p. 6); capability checking (p. 8). Central component: no single component is stated. Whether privilege servers must agree: not stated. **Scheduling:** "a fleet which manages process scheduling and layout" (p. 6); "Scheduling becomes a layout problem not a time multiplexing problem" (p. 5); "spatially aware placement engine/scheduler" (p. 2). Central: not stated. **Resource allocation:** "a fleet which manages physical memory allocation" (p. 6). Devices: the OS layer provides "management of system resources such as cores, memory, and input-output devices" (p. 6), with no mechanism given. Central: not stated. **Naming:** the name server fleet holds "the canonical mailbox name to physical core and mailbox directory", cached per microkernel (p. 6), inspired by "the hierarchical caching in the Internet's DNS system" (p. 9). Central: not stated (a canonical directory over a fleet implies coordination (inferred)). **Failure handling:** "broken servers can be steered away from when a fault is detected"; "fos is primarily focused on scalability and not fault tolerance" (p. 6). **Cost of decentralising:** "Writing fos servers can be more challenging than writing traditional shared memory operating system subsystems" (p. 5); in message passing "the destination of any piece of data must be known when a message is sent" (p. 8); for lock servers, "the cost of software-based lock management may dwarf the performance wins of removing traditional locks" (p. 8); whether shared structures like the buffer cache perform well is an "open question" (p. 8). | p. 2, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 |
| Cost of message primitives | Not measured for fos. The paper cites figures from other systems: "Typical context switch times are in the 100 cycle to 300 cycle range on modern processors" (no source given), and on Raw and Tilera "the cost of core-to-core dynamic messages is on the order of 15 - 45 cycles depending on distance" ([21, 24, 25]). Tag: design figure (cited, not measured in this paper). | p. 8 |
| Performance results | (1) Metric: cycles (billions) per core to complete a fixed per-core workload. Workload: allocate 1 GB and write the first byte of each page, 1–16 cores. System: Linux 2.6.24.7 on a Dell PowerEdge R900 with 4× Intel Xeon E7340 at 2.40 GHz and 16 GB. Baseline: hypothetical perfect scaling (equal bar heights). Values: about 0.8 at 1 core, about 4 at 8 cores, about 12 at 16 cores (read off, Fig. 1). Text: "Beyond eight processors, the addition of more processors actually slows down the computation" (measured; p. 3). (2) Metric: cache miss rate (%) split into user, OS/user interference and OS. Workload: Apache2 on Linux 2.6.18.8 / Debian 4 serving static pages to Apache Bench "simulating ten concurrent users". Setup: QEMU x86_64-based cache model, direct-mapped and two-way caches from 1024 to 262144 bytes. Values: direct-mapped total about 21% at 1024 B, falling to about 1.5% at 262144 B, with the OS band the largest part at small sizes; two-way total about 16.5% at 1024 B (read off, Figs. 2–3; simulated). Text: "for small cache sizes, the miss rates for the operating system far surpass the miss rates for the application" (p. 4). fos: no performance result. | p. 3, 4 |
| Scaling | Linux 2.6.24.7 page allocator: 1–16 cores measured; per-core cycles grow from about 0.8 to about 12 billion (read off, Fig. 1); "does not scale beyond 8 cores under heavy load" (measured; p. 2–3). Baseline: hypothetical perfect scaling. fos: not measured. The prototype boots on 16 cores and in QEMU with up to 255 (p. 8); the design target is "1000+ core systems" (p. 2) and scaling "across a large range (> 3 orders of decimal magnitude) of core count" (p. 5). | p. 2, 3, 5, 8 |
| Attributed causes | (1) "as the number of cores increases, the lock contention begins to dominate the execution time" (p. 3); "the top level re-balancing lock ends up being the scalability problem" (p. 3–4). Stated by the fos designers about a third-party system (Linux). They say it needs "some algorithmic rethinking" because the code "is already quite fine-grain locked" (p. 4), i.e. inherent to the lock-based design (their reading). Isolated: partly, by an oprofile breakdown per function (Fig. 1). (2) Architectural overhead "is believed to be caused by contention in the hardware memory system" (p. 3). Hedged; not isolated. (3) Interference misses from OS and application sharing a core: "This interference can be removed completely when the operating system and application is executed in different cores" (p. 4). Isolated by simulating separate caches (simulated). (4) Expected fos benefits, such as no context swap when an application messages an OS server (p. 9) and no shared-memory locks between cores (p. 7). Asserted by the designers; not measured. | p. 3, 4, 7, 9 |
| Fate and reasons | Not stated in this paper. At writing: "The operating system is under active development" (p. 2, p. 8). | p. 2, 8 |
| Concurrency defects | n/a (I1) | — |
| What shapes programs | n/a (I1). See Notes for the paper's claims about locks and message passing shaping OS code. | — |
| Hardware–language trade-off | n/a (I1) | — |
| Model equivalence | n/a (I1). See Notes: fos messages may be carried over shared memory. | — |
| Model mixing | n/a (I1). See Notes: applications may mix shared memory and messaging. | — |
| Runtime limits | n/a (I1) | — |
| Many-core scaling | Core counts: prototype on 16-core x86_64 and QEMU up to 255 (p. 8); target 1000+ (p. 2). Shared memory and coherence: the x86_64 platform has it (inferred from p. 4), but the fos OS layer does not use it (p. 6). Inter-core communication: microkernel messaging to named mailboxes, transported "via on-chip networks or shared memory" (p. 6). Scaling result: none for fos; the Linux allocator folds back beyond 8 cores (p. 3). Limits named: locks and lock granularity, with Amdahl's law invoked by name ("Ahmdal's law", no reference; p. 2–3); cache coherence ("Hardware directory based cache coherence has found difficulties providing high performance cache coherent shared memory above about 100 cores", p. 5); locality and cache interference (p. 4); "the abstraction of a global shared memory space is inherently a global shared structure" (p. 2). Power is named only as a reason clock frequency stopped rising (p. 1). | p. 1–6, 8 |
| Adoption factors | n/a (I1) | — |
| Quality | See the Quality table above. | p. 1–10 |
| Notes | See Notes. | — |

## Concepts
| Concept | What the paper says | Page |
|---|---|---|
| factored operating system (fos) (new) | An OS "factored into function specific services", each "distributed into spatially distributed servers" that "collaborate and communicate only via message passing" | p. 5 |
| space multiplexing replaces time multiplexing (new) | "Scheduling becomes a layout problem not a time multiplexing problem"; the OS "runs on distinct cores from applications" | p. 5 |
| fleet (new) | The set of servers of one type that together provide one OS function, e.g. physical memory allocation, file system, scheduling | p. 6 |
| fos client (new) | "The code executing on a single core under the fos-microkernel"; applications and OS servers "act as peers" | p. 6 |
| receive mailbox (new) | A named, protected endpoint owned by a client, with a large buffer in the receiver's address space; a send to a full mailbox returns an error | p. 6, 8 |
| message proxy library / translation library (new) | Turns a traditional system call into a message to an OS-layer server and unpacks the reply | p. 6–7 |
| microkernel to OS layer delegation (new) | The microkernel delegates naming and privilege to OS-layer fleets, caches their answers, and avoids cycles by knowing the delegates' locations and granting static privileges ("privilege fixed point") | p. 7 |
| stateless, transaction-oriented server with continuations (new) | A server processes each transaction to completion without preemption, stores a continuation for long-latency operations, and needs no local locking | p. 7 |
| notional lock / lock server (new) | A lock held by a server and acquired by message; "the cost of software-based lock management may dwarf the performance wins of removing traditional locks" | p. 8 |
| OS-application and OS-OS locality aliasing (new) | OS and application working sets competing for implicitly shared caches and TLBs on one core, including "anti-locality cache collisions" | p. 4 |
| best-effort OS interfaces (new) | Interfaces that return information "which may be slightly out of date" for higher performance, with an accurate but slower alternative | p. 2 |

## Notes
- **Source and version:** author preprint PDF, downloaded on 2026-10-07 from https://www.princeton.edu/~wentzlaf/documents/Wentzlaff.2009.OSR.fos.pdf and saved as `papers/P102.pdf` (11 pages, created 2009-03-02, marked "To appear in ACM SIGOPS Operating System Review ... April 2009", p. 1). The ACM PDF returned 403, and Unpaywall lists no open-access copy. The publisher page range 76–85 is from Crossref. Read in full, figures included (second pass).
- **Criterion:** the full text meets I1(c) as screened. The OS layer's servers "communicate only via the messaging interface provided by the microkernel layer" (p. 6), the paper uses the terms "message passing", "send" and "mailbox" (p. 5–6), and fos runs without an underlying conventional kernel (p. 5). No exclusion applies. X2 does not: messaging is the kernel's own mechanism, not a library on a conventional kernel. X3 does not: the target is a single multicore chip (p. 9). X5 does not: a 10-page journal article. The paper may also answer SQ13/SQ14 under I4 (inferred), through its Linux scaling measurements and its named limits of cache-coherent shared memory (p. 3, p. 5). That would not change the include verdict.
- **For SQ10 (model equivalence, I4 field):** fos messages may be carried on shared memory: "The fos-microkernels transport the message to the destination via on-chip networks or shared memory" (p. 6). The cost of doing so is not reported.
- **For SQ11 (model mixing):** "Within an application, communication can be achieved via shared memory communication or messaging", and fos keeps shared memory for applications "if the underlying hardware supports it" (p. 6).
- **For SQ7/SQ8 (defects, what shapes programs):** the paper argues, without counts, that "Adding locks into an operating system is time consuming and error prone" and that locks "can introduce circular dependencies and hence cause deadlocks" (p. 3). It also argues that "global shared memory easily allows the introduction of data races which can be difficult to detect at test time" (p. 5). It expects that "the shared nothing, message passing only, approach will encourage OS developers to think very carefully about exactly what data is being shared" (p. 5). It says "the message passing nature of fos discourages this usage model [lock managers] by making programming in this manner difficult" (p. 7). All of these are argument, not measurement.
- **Open questions the authors name:** whether shared OS structures (virtual memory, buffer cache) "can be accessed with good performance" (p. 8); whether all multi-sequence operations can be written without local locks: "it is not certain that all cases can be handled" (p. 8); whether "a hardware solution or the software solution explored by fos proves more scalable" (p. 8).

# Agent contract

What every agent in `.claude/agents/` does, whatever its role. The agent's own file adds only its role.

## You receive
From the step skill that dispatched you:
- **Row:** the flow row you run (e.g. `3a`), defined in `ai/flow-sls.md` or `ai/flow-dsrm.md`.
- **Inputs:** the exact files you read. Paths are relative to `research/` unless they start with `ai/` or `artifact/`.
- **Outputs:** the exact files you write.

## You do
1. Read the row in its flow file, then every input file. Read nothing else from `research/`; your view of the research is the inputs.
2. For each output, copy its template from `ai/template/` (the table in `ai/template/README.md` maps output to template) and fill every `{placeholder}`.
3. Set the frontmatter: `id`, `row`, `by:` your agent name, `status: proposed`, `inputs:` the files you read.
4. Write only the output files. Every other file, and every `status`, belongs to me.

## Your output is done when
- Every output file exists and has every section of its template.
- No `{placeholder}` or `[ ]` is left. A field you cannot fill says why, in one line.
- Every claim about a paper carries its P ID and page, or the reference and page for papers not yet in the review.
- Every fact comes from a file or source you actually read in this run. A fact you cannot trace to one is left out and named in your report.

## You return
A short report to the skill:
- Each file written, with one line on what it holds.
- Open issues: fields you could not fill, sources you could not reach, decisions you found that are mine to make.
- Each decision that is mine as a choice: two to four concrete options, the exact edit each one makes to which file, and the one you recommend. The gate asks me with these (`ai/gate.md`).

# P49

## Reference
Tanenbaum, A. S., Herder, J. N., Bos, H. (2006). *Can We Make Operating Systems Reliable and Secure?*. IEEE Computer 39(5) (May 2006), pp. 44–51, cover feature. https://doi.org/10.1109/mc.2006.156. P49, round-file row R0-067; screened include under I1. The full text meets I1(c) (see Notes). Version read: publisher layout ("Published by the IEEE Computer Society", "0018-9162/06/$20.00 © 2006 IEEE", p. 44), 8 PDF pages, taken from https://minix3.org/docs/jorrit-herder/computer-may06.pdf and saved as `papers/P49.pdf`. Pages cited are the printed ones: printed page = PDF page + 43 (PDF page 1 = p. 44, PDF page 8 = p. 51). The volume number 39(5) is not printed on the pages (inferred from "May 2006").

## Deepest pass
2 (whole text read, every section, figure caption and reference; the authors' claims were not checked against the cited design papers, so not a third pass)

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** A magazine argument comparing "four different approaches that researchers are using to make future operating systems more reliable and secure, proceeding from the least radical to the most radical solution" (p. 45): Nooks, paravirtual machines on L4, multiserver operating systems (Minix 3), and language-based protection (Singularity). It is a position or analytical argument with a design description of the authors' own Minix 3 (pp. 47–49), not a primary research paper.
- **Context:** Operating systems are "huge" and have "very poor fault isolation" (p. 44); bug density figures from cited studies [1, 2, 3] are used to estimate kernel bug counts (p. 44). Builds on Nooks [4, 5], L4 and L4Linux [7, 8, 9], Minix 3 [10], Singularity (no citation given) and the Burroughs B5000 (p. 49).
- **Correctness:** The bug estimates assume bug count scales with lines of code, at "a conservative estimate of six bugs per 1,000 lines" taken from other code bases (pp. 44, 48); this is an assumption, not a measurement of these kernels. Performance claims for Minix 3 are given in one paragraph without baseline version or run counts (p. 49); the paravirtualization overhead "about 3 to 8 percent" is attributed to "performance measurements" with no citation or setup (p. 47).
- **Contributions:** (1) a side-by-side description of four approaches to OS reliability (pp. 45–50); (2) the observation that three of the four "use microkernels" and that microkernels "might be making a comeback due to their potentially higher reliability" (p. 50); (3) a description of Minix 3's message-passing IPC, its integration of interrupts with message passing, and its reincarnation server (pp. 47–49).
- **Clarity:** Clear and well organised by approach; written for a general audience, so mechanisms are described only at the level of principle.

## Quality
| Q | Answer | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | yes | Stated in one place: "Here we address four different approaches ... proceeding from the least radical to the most radical solution" (p. 45). |
| Q2 | partly | For Minix 3: "fixed-length messages", "rendezvous principle", direct copy when "both the sender and the receiver are ready", undeliverable events "marked pending a bitmap" (p. 48); how receivers are named is not described beyond "allowed destinations" (p. 48). Singularity channels get message typing and protocol (pp. 49–50) but no buffering or busy-receiver behaviour. |
| Q3 | yes | The authors' own figures come from Minix 3, a kernel that runs real programs and "can build itself" (p. 49); figures for Nooks and L4 are reported from others' work (pp. 46–47). |
| Q4 | partly | Minix 3's loss is measured against "in-kernel drivers" with no named system or version (p. 49); the 6-second build and the 3–8 percent paravirtualization overhead name no baseline (pp. 47, 49). |
| Q5 | partly | The build gives workload ("112 compilations and 11 links") and hardware ("2.2-GHz Athlon"), but no run count and no reason for the workload (p. 49); the "less than 10 percent" figure has no setup at all (p. 49). |
| Q6 | n/a | Cannot apply: the standfirst (abstract) and the conclusion make no quantitative claim, only that microkernels have "lower performance" and "potentially higher reliability" (pp. 44, 50). |
| Q7 | partly | The user-mode driver overhead is isolated by comparing against in-kernel drivers (p. 49); other causes ("eliminates kernel traps and context switches", p. 49; reliability from kernel size and static data structures, p. 48) are only asserted. |
| Q8 | partly | A dedicated "Limitations" subsection exists only for Nooks (p. 46); Minix 3's limits are mentioned in passing ("currently only servers that do not maintain much internal state can be restarted", p. 48; restarting "will not remove the bug", p. 48); no threats to validity for the article's own claims. |
| Q9 | partly | Herder is the first author of the cited Minix 3 design paper [10] (p. 51), and Minix 3 is the only system the article itself measures (p. 49); no author is listed as a designer of Nooks, L4 or Singularity. Whether Tanenbaum and Bos built Minix 3 is not stated in the paper (inferred likely). |

## Extracted fields
| Field | Value | Page |
|---|---|---|
| Reference | Tanenbaum, Herder, Bos (2006), *Can We Make Operating Systems Reliable and Secure?*, IEEE Computer, May 2006, pp. 44–51; P49; I1 (I1(c), see Notes). Publisher layout; printed page = PDF page + 43 | 44, 51 |
| Paper type | Position or analytical argument (comparison of four approaches, conclusion that microkernels "might be making a comeback"); design (description of Minix 3) | 45, 47–49, 50 |
| System | (1) Nooks, on Linux, by "the Nooks team" [4, 5]; status: running (inferred from "experiments show", p. 46). (2) L4 microkernel built "in the 1990s" by "a research group at the University of Karlsruhe", with L4Linux and driver virtual machines [7, 8, 9]; running kernel (inferred). (3) Minix 3, multiserver OS, builders not named in the text (design paper by Herder et al. [10]); running kernel, "available for free download under the Berkeley license", for the Pentium. (4) Singularity, by "Microsoft Research", year not stated; status not stated. (5) Burroughs B5000, mentioned as historical precedent only | 46, 47, 49 |
| Levels with message semantics | Kernel, Minix 3: partly. Between OS processes, messages are the only stated path: servers and drivers "cannot directly call each other's functions or share data structures. Instead, Minix 3 performs IPC by passing fixed-length messages"; user library calls "do their work by sending messages to servers"; interrupts are turned into messages ("the kernel turns it into a normal message"). Other paths: "kernel calls" from drivers and servers (whether these are messages is not stated), and "The clock driver shares the microkernel's address space". Kernel, Singularity: partly. "all process-to-process communication uses these channels" and user processes "obtain system services by sending strongly typed messages to the microkernel", but a "shared object heap" is an exception and the microkernel "handles thread synchronization with mutexes". Language (Sing#): partly, "augmented with message passing primitives" and "fully supports channels in the language". Instruction set and hardware: not stated (Pentium with MMU, x86). Between cores versus within a core: not stated; the paper does not discuss multiprocessors. Started message-based and later added non-message paths: for Singularity the heap is presented as a design exception made because channels alone "would be very slow"; no history of later additions is stated | 47, 48, 49, 50 |
| Receiving unit and state ownership | Minix 3: process (driver, server or user process), each "in its own private address space, protected by the memory management unit (MMU) hardware"; others reach its memory only through "kernel calls (which the kernel inspects for validity)"; the clock driver shares the kernel's address space. Singularity: process, "a closed entity" with its own code, data, runtime and garbage collector; all processes in "a single virtual address space"; isolation by the compiler ("will not allow a process to touch another process's data"); objects on the shared heap belong to "a single process" at each instant, and "ownership of an object can be passed over a channel" | 47, 48, 49, 50 |
| Message mechanism | Minix 3: synchronous "rendezvous principle: When both the sender and the receiver are ready, the system copies the message directly from the sender to the receiver"; "fixed-length messages"; "does not require message queuing or buffering"; "an asynchronous event notification mechanism is available. Events that cannot be delivered are marked pending a bitmap in the process table"; interrupt handlers set a bit in the driver's "pending interrupts" bitmap "and then continue without blocking"; naming: per-process "allowed destinations" (how destinations are named is not stated); user processes "can use only the rendezvous principle and can send to only the Posix servers"; dispatch: not stated. Singularity: "strongly typed messages" over "point-to-point bidirectional channels"; a channel contract declares message types and a state machine for the protocol (example contract C1); synchrony, buffering and busy-receiver behaviour not stated | 48, 49, 50 |
| Non-message primitives | Minix 3: "kernel calls" for privileged operations such as "reading a selected portion of a specific user's address space or writing to authorized I/O ports" (reason: drivers in user mode "cannot execute privileged instructions or read or write the computer's I/O ports"); clock driver sharing the microkernel's address space (no reason given); interrupts, handled by the microkernel and converted to notifications; MMU protection. Singularity: "shared object heap" (reason: "If all data, such as file blocks read from disk, had to go over channels, the system would be very slow"); "mutexes" for thread synchronization in the microkernel (no reason given); MMU used "only to map pages"; trusted hardware abstraction layer hiding "I/O ports, interrupt request lines, direct memory access channels, and timers" | 47, 48, 49, 50 |
| Self-definition | Singularity: "written almost entirely in Sing#", but of its microkernel "a small portion is written in C#, C++, or assembler and must be trusted since it cannot be verified"; this trusted code "includes the hardware abstraction layer and the garbage collector" (cost of that base: it cannot be verified). Running inspection or change: the design "forbids dynamic process extensions" and "does not permit loadable modules"; components carry metadata used by "External verifiers" before execution. Minix 3: implementation language not stated; no reflection stated | 49, 50 |
| Interposition | Nooks: yes between kernel and driver: "the call actually goes to a wrapper that checks the parameters for validity and manages the call"; goal "as few changes as possible to existing drivers and the kernel" (so not strictly "without changing either"); stubs generated automatically, bodies handwritten, "455 wrappers"; isolation via "the virtual memory page map"; shadow drivers log driver–kernel communication; cost not stated. Paravirtual machines: drivers "do not have to be modified" but the Linux kernel is ("about 3,000 lines of code" added to it for I/O), plus "An additional 5,000 lines of code" for communication between the driver VMs and the application VM; overhead "about 3 to 8 percent". Minix 3: the kernel's per-process bitmaps can block sends (for example "sending messages to the audio driver"), which is filtering, not interposition of a third component (inferred); placing a component between Minix 3 processes: not stated | 45, 46, 47, 48 |
| Operating system functions | Minix 3. Protection: MMU address spaces plus "bitmaps and ranges within the kernel's process table" controlling permitted kernel calls, IPC capabilities and I/O ports; central component yes (the kernel's process table). Scheduling: the microkernel "performs process scheduling"; central yes. Resource allocation: "the process manager, which handles process and memory management"; device access through kernel calls; central yes (single process manager, inferred from the text). Naming: "the data store, a simple name server that the other servers use"; central yes. Failure handling: the "reincarnation server, which is the parent process of all the other servers and all the drivers", restarts failed drivers and servers; central yes. Singularity: the microkernel "controls access to hardware; allocates and deallocates memory; creates, destroys, and schedules threads"; naming by "a single hierarchical name space" with "A root name server" at the top and mountable name servers; protection by language safety and three-step verification; central components yes (microkernel, root name server). Cost or loss of a decentralised version: not stated | 47, 48, 49, 50 |
| Cost of message primitives | not stated (no latency or cycle count for one send or switch is given) | 48–50 |
| Performance results | (a) Minix 3, metric: performance loss, user-mode drivers vs "in-kernel drivers", value "less than 10 percent" (measured (inferred); workload and baseline version not stated). (b) Minix 3 self-build ("kernel, common drivers, and all servers (112 compilations and 11 links)"), time "less than 6 seconds on a 2.2-GHz Athlon processor" (measured (inferred)); no baseline. (c) Paravirtualized driver VMs on L4: overhead "about 3 to 8 percent" ("Performance measurements have shown"; workload, baseline and source not stated). (d) Nooks: "can catch 99 percent of the fatal driver errors and 55 percent of the nonfatal ones" ("experiments show"; setup not stated). (e) Bug estimates, analytical: Linux kernel "something like 15,000 bugs", Windows XP "at least double", Minix 3 kernel (about 4,000 lines) "probably only about 24", all at six bugs per 1,000 lines | 44, 46, 47, 48, 49 |
| Scaling | not stated (no core or node counts measured) | — |
| Attributed causes | (1) Microkernel ideas were "not fully explored the first time around because it has slightly lower performance than a monolithic kernel. In the 1980s, performance counted for everything" (designers of Minix 3; not isolated by measurement; about the history of the design, inherent per the paper). (2) Minix 3's user-mode drivers: "While introducing a small amount of overhead, this design also enhances reliability" (designers; overhead isolated by comparison with in-kernel drivers, p. 49; inherent to the design (inferred)). (3) Minix 3 "has not been optimized for performance" yet "is reasonably fast" (designers; implementation; not isolated). (4) Singularity's single address space gives "efficiency—because it eliminates kernel traps and context switches" (third party, about Microsoft's design; inherent; not measured in the paper). (5) Singularity: channels alone "would be very slow" for bulk data, hence the shared heap (third party; inherent; not measured). (6) Paravirtual overhead about 3–8 percent: cause not stated | 47, 49, 50 |
| Fate and reasons | Minix 3: "available for free download under the Berkeley license"; "Ports to other architectures and to embedded systems are under development" (designers). Microkernels in general: "long discarded as unacceptable because of their lower performance compared with monolithic kernels" and "might be making a comeback due to their potentially higher reliability, which many people now regard as more important than performance"; "It is not yet known which, if any, of these approaches will be widely adopted in the long run" (stated by Minix 3's designers about the field). Nooks, L4 paravirtualization, Singularity: research projects; fate not stated | 44, 47, 49, 50 |

## Concepts

| new: channel contract | Sing# channels with "formal typing and protocol specifications": declared messages and a state machine for the protocol | 49–50 |
| new: single-owner shared heap | "at each instant every object on the heap belongs to a single process. However, ownership of an object can be passed over a channel", allowing zero-copy I/O | 50 |

- **Source:** full text, publisher layout of IEEE Computer, May 2006, pp. 44–51, from https://minix3.org/docs/jorrit-herder/computer-may06.pdf (8 PDF pages), saved as `papers/P49.pdf`. Unpaywall lists the DOI as closed access.

The Burroughs B5000 is cited as protection "handled not by an MMU ... but by the Algol compiler's refusal to generate 'dangerous' code" (p. 49), relevant to *Hardware–language trade-off* if the paper were also included under I4.

# Selection criteria

A paper is included if it meets at least one inclusion criterion and no exclusion criterion. Each verdict names the criterion that decided it. There is no restriction on publication date. "Message-based" in these criteria means: meets I1.

Terms used in the criteria and the SQs:
- **Below the programming language:** in the operating system kernel, the instruction set, microcode or hardware; not in a language runtime, library or virtual machine hosted on a conventional kernel (as in X2).
- **Written in its own objects and messages:** the level's code is objects receiving messages in the system's own model, not a lower language, microcode or hardware outside that model.
- **Without changing either:** neither the sender's nor the receiver's code, nor how they name each other, is modified to place the component between them.

| ID | Inclusion criterion |
|---|---|
| I1 | A paper is included if it describes, implements, simulates or evaluates a processor, instruction set, microarchitecture, multicomputer node or operating system kernel in which sending a message, invoking a method on an object, or delivering a message to an actor is a primitive of that level, i.e. one of: (a) an instruction of the instruction set; (b) a hardware or microcode mechanism; (c) for a kernel, the stated means by which the kernel and its system services, or the kernel's own parts, communicate (as in microkernels, multikernels, or operating systems written in an object or actor language that run without an underlying conventional kernel). The paper must name the mechanism with at least one of these terms: message, message passing, send, mailbox, actor, active message, inter-process communication (IPC), method invocation. (SQ1–SQ5) |
| I2 | A paper is included if it is a retrospective, evaluation or historical account of at least one computer architecture that its authors describe as directed at a high-level language, object-based, object-oriented or message-driven, and it reports either measured performance of that architecture or a stated reason for its performance, adoption, abandonment, or becoming unnecessary. (SQ5, SQ6) |
| I3 | A paper is included if it is an empirical study of concurrency defects (bugs) in real programs or systems (not only examples written by the authors) and it reports counts or proportions of defects either split by communication mechanism (shared memory versus message passing) or for programs or systems built on message passing only, or for programs or systems built on shared memory only, as the comparison baseline for SQ7. Programs whose defects are reported as accesses to shared variables count as shared-memory programs even if the paper does not use that term. (SQ7) |
| I4 | A paper is included if it reports evidence or an argument that directly answers one of SQ8–SQ19, whether or not it mentions messages or objects. (SQ8–SQ19) |

| ID | Exclusion criterion |
|---|---|
| X1 | A paper is excluded if it meets none of I1, I2, I3, I4. |
| X2 | A paper included only through I1 is excluded if message passing appears only at the application, library, language runtime, virtual machine or network-protocol level, running on a processor whose instruction set and hardware have no message mechanism and on a kernel that fails I1(c) (e.g. an actor library, the Erlang virtual machine, a Message Passing Interface library, a Smalltalk virtual machine hosted on Unix or Windows). Does not apply to papers that meet I2 or I3. |
| X3 | A paper is excluded if the system is a cluster or network of separate computers, each with a processor whose instruction set and hardware have no message mechanism and a kernel that fails I1(c), and the message mechanism lies only in the network interface or interconnect between them. |
| X4 | A paper is excluded if the hardware it presents is stated to serve only a fixed function or domain (e.g. neural-network inference, signal processing, packet switching, graphics) and is not stated to run general programs. Does not apply to papers included through I4. |
| X5 | A paper is excluded if it is not one of: journal article; conference or workshop paper longer than 2 pages; book or book chapter; doctoral or master's thesis; technical report of a university, company research laboratory or standards body; magazine article of a professional society (Association for Computing Machinery, Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, USENIX); architecture or system reference manual published by the system's manufacturer. Patents, slides, posters, extended abstracts of 2 pages or fewer, blog posts, forum posts, encyclopaedia entries and product brochures are excluded. |
| X6 | A paper is excluded if its full text is in neither English nor Spanish. |
| X7 | A paper is excluded if its full text cannot be obtained from the publisher, an author's or institution's web page, arXiv, Semantic Scholar, the Internet Archive, or the university library. The sources tried are recorded with the verdict. |
| X8 | A paper is excluded if it reports the same system and the same results as another included paper. The one with more pages is kept; the other is excluded unless it reports at least one measurement, design element or stated reason absent from the kept one. |
| X9 | A paper is excluded if its title or abstract presents it as a survey, review, overview or taxonomy of other work and it reports no measurement and states no reason under I2 of its own. Its reference list is still used for snowballing. |
---

# Data extraction form

Fields filled for every included paper (`sls/3-reading/P*.md`). Every SQ is served by at least one field.

- **Applies to:** a field applies to papers included under the criteria in its *Applies to* column; for I4, only the fields serving the SQs the paper answers. A field that does not apply is written `n/a (I3)` (the paper's criterion). `not stated` means the field applies but the paper is silent.
- **Values:** every number in *Cost of message primitives*, *Performance results* and *Scaling* is tagged `measured`, `simulated`, `design figure`, `analytical` or `read off` (estimated from a plot).

| Field | What to record | Serves | Applies to |
|---|---|---|---|
| Reference | Authors, year, title, venue, pages; P ID; criteria that included it (I1–I4). Pages cited in the record are those printed on `papers/P*.pdf` (else its PDF page); say which version it is (publisher, preprint, manuscript, reprint), give the publisher's page range and any offset. ## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** Design and evaluation of a processor architecture and its run-time software, SOAR ("Smalltalk On A RISC"). It also contains a survey of earlier high-level-language machines (Ch. 2) and a new garbage collector, Generation Scavenging (Ch. 5) (pp. 1–5).
- **Context:** Smalltalk-80 runs poorly on widely available hardware. The only machine that "has demonstrated universally acceptable Smalltalk-80 performance" is the $120,000 ECL Xerox Dorado (p. 11). Earlier language machines (R-2, Burroughs B5700/B6700, Scheme-79, Symbolics 3600, Katana-32) "closely coupled the source language semantics to the hardware" (p. 14). RISC work (IBM 801, RISC I/II, MIPS) and the Deutsch-Schiffman software techniques for the 68010 are the other context (pp. 12–14, 24–28).
- **Correctness:** The premise is that a RISC with a few Smalltalk-specific additions can match microcoded or high-level-instruction machines. It is tested by instruction-level simulation of Xerox's official benchmarks (pp. 61–66). The NMOS chip exists and ran diagnostics, but Smalltalk-80 had not yet run on it (pp. 2, 127). The value of each feature is an omission cost measured in cycles under the current compiler. The author says this neglects cycle-time effects and compiler interaction (pp. 64–65, 67, 72).
- **Contributions:** (1) The SOAR instruction set, with tagged integer arithmetic, register windows, in-line call-target caching, fast shuffle, trap mechanisms and direct object pointers (Ch. 3). (2) A feature-by-feature evaluation that sorts features into "winners", "questionable" and "losers" (Tables 4.4–4.5, pp. 68–69). (3) Generation Scavenging, which reclaims storage with about 3% CPU overhead and no object table (Ch. 5, p. 126). (4) The "architect's trap" lesson (p. 70).
- **Clarity:** Clearly written and organised, with summary tables per chapter. The scan is legible but OCR-noisy, and a few table cells were checked against page images (pp. 66, 71).

- **Chapters read:** front matter and abstract; Ch. 1 (pp. 1–5); Ch. 2 (pp. 6–29); Ch. 3 (pp. 30–60); Ch. 4 (pp. 61–73); Ch. 5 §5.1–5.2, §5.9.3–5.11 (pp. 74–75, 101–110); Ch. 7 (pp. 125–129); Appendix A §A.4.4–A.4.5 (pp. 185–192). Not read: Ch. 5 §5.3–5.9.2 (algorithm survey and detailed GS evaluation), Ch. 6 (medium-lifetime objects, analytical), and the rest of Appendices A and B (raw data).
- **Criterion:** the full text supports I2 as screened. SOAR is described as an architecture for the Smalltalk-80 language, with simulated performance and stated reasons (pp. 2, 61–73). It does not meet I1: SOAR has no send or message instruction or mechanism (Table 3.2 p. 37), and sends are compiled to `call` plus software lookup (pp. 46–47). No verdict change proposed.
- **Discrepancy (Q6):** the abstract (PDF p. 8) says the language-specific hardware "doubles its performance over a RISC II with the same cycle time". Table 4.6 and p. 71 give a ratio of 1.6. Elsewhere the paper says the language-specific features "approximately double performance" (p. 4), and that register windows and tagged integers "nearly double SOAR's performance" (p. 125). These may measure different things. I record them as stated.
- **Evidence status:** most performance figures are cycle counts from simulation multiplied by 400 ns. The chips' effective cycle is 510 ns, and the chip ran diagnostics at 800 ns actual system cycle time (Table 3.8 p. 59; p. 127). So the "as fast as a Dorado" claim is a prediction: "the 400 ns NMOS SOAR chips that have been fabricated should run just as fast" (p. 73).
- **Process model:** process switches are deferred to safe calls and jumps through a software interrupt. All Smalltalk processes share one address space (pp. 45–46). This is relevant to SQ2 as a non-message, shared-memory base beneath the object model.

# Selection criteria

A paper is included if it meets at least one inclusion criterion and no exclusion criterion. Each verdict names the criterion that decided it. There is no restriction on publication date. "Message-based" in these criteria means: meets I1.

Terms used in the criteria and the SQs:
- **Below the programming language:** in the operating system kernel, the instruction set, microcode or hardware; not in a language runtime, library or virtual machine hosted on a conventional kernel (as in X2).
- **Written in its own objects and messages:** the level's code is objects receiving messages in the system's own model, not a lower language, microcode or hardware outside that model.
- **Without changing either:** neither the sender's nor the receiver's code, nor how they name each other, is modified to place the component between them.

| ID | Inclusion criterion |
|---|---|
| I1 | A paper is included if it describes, implements, simulates or evaluates a processor, instruction set, microarchitecture, multicomputer node or operating system kernel in which sending a message, invoking a method on an object, or delivering a message to an actor is a primitive of that level, i.e. one of: (a) an instruction of the instruction set; (b) a hardware or microcode mechanism; (c) for a kernel, the stated means by which the kernel and its system services, or the kernel's own parts, communicate (as in microkernels, multikernels, or operating systems written in an object or actor language that run without an underlying conventional kernel). The paper must name the mechanism with at least one of these terms: message, message passing, send, mailbox, actor, active message, inter-process communication (IPC), method invocation. (SQ1–SQ5) |
| I2 | A paper is included if it is a retrospective, evaluation or historical account of at least one computer architecture that its authors describe as directed at a high-level language, object-based, object-oriented or message-driven, and it reports either measured performance of that architecture or a stated reason for its performance, adoption, abandonment, or becoming unnecessary. (SQ5, SQ6) |
| I3 | A paper is included if it is an empirical study of concurrency defects (bugs) in real programs or systems (not only examples written by the authors) and it reports counts or proportions of defects either split by communication mechanism (shared memory versus message passing) or for programs or systems built on message passing only, or for programs or systems built on shared memory only, as the comparison baseline for SQ7. Programs whose defects are reported as accesses to shared variables count as shared-memory programs even if the paper does not use that term. (SQ7) |
| I4 | A paper is included if it reports evidence or an argument that directly answers one of SQ8–SQ19, whether or not it mentions messages or objects. (SQ8–SQ19) |

| ID | Exclusion criterion |
|---|---|
| X1 | A paper is excluded if it meets none of I1, I2, I3, I4. |
| X2 | A paper included only through I1 is excluded if message passing appears only at the application, library, language runtime, virtual machine or network-protocol level, running on a processor whose instruction set and hardware have no message mechanism and on a kernel that fails I1(c) (e.g. an actor library, the Erlang virtual machine, a Message Passing Interface library, a Smalltalk virtual machine hosted on Unix or Windows). Does not apply to papers that meet I2 or I3. |
| X3 | A paper is excluded if the system is a cluster or network of separate computers, each with a processor whose instruction set and hardware have no message mechanism and a kernel that fails I1(c), and the message mechanism lies only in the network interface or interconnect between them. |
| X4 | A paper is excluded if the hardware it presents is stated to serve only a fixed function or domain (e.g. neural-network inference, signal processing, packet switching, graphics) and is not stated to run general programs. Does not apply to papers included through I4. |
| X5 | A paper is excluded if it is not one of: journal article; conference or workshop paper longer than 2 pages; book or book chapter; doctoral or master's thesis; technical report of a university, company research laboratory or standards body; magazine article of a professional society (Association for Computing Machinery, Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, USENIX); architecture or system reference manual published by the system's manufacturer. Patents, slides, posters, extended abstracts of 2 pages or fewer, blog posts, forum posts, encyclopaedia entries and product brochures are excluded. |
| X6 | A paper is excluded if its full text is in neither English nor Spanish. |
| X7 | A paper is excluded if its full text cannot be obtained from the publisher, an author's or institution's web page, arXiv, Semantic Scholar, the Internet Archive, or the university library. The sources tried are recorded with the verdict. |
| X8 | A paper is excluded if it reports the same system and the same results as another included paper. The one with more pages is kept; the other is excluded unless it reports at least one measurement, design element or stated reason absent from the kept one. |
| X9 | A paper is excluded if its title or abstract presents it as a survey, review, overview or taxonomy of other work and it reports no measurement and states no reason under I2 of its own. Its reference list is still used for snowballing. |

# Data extraction form

Fields filled for every included paper (`sls/3-reading/P*.md`). Every SQ is served by at least one field.

- **Applies to:** a field applies to papers included under the criteria in its *Applies to* column; for I4, only the fields serving the SQs the paper answers. A field that does not apply is written `n/a (I3)` (the paper's criterion). `not stated` means the field applies but the paper is silent.
- **Values:** every number in *Cost of message primitives*, *Performance results* and *Scaling* is tagged `measured`, `simulated`, `design figure`, `analytical` or `read off` (estimated from a plot).

| Field | What to record | Serves | Applies to |
|---|---|---|---|
| Reference | Authors, year, title, venue, pages; P ID; criteria that included it (I1–I4). Pages cited in the record are those printed on `papers/P*.pdf` (else its PDF page); say which version it is (publisher, preprint, manuscript, reprint), give the publisher's page range and any offset. Content taken from an abstract only cites `abstract` | SQ1–SQ19 | all |
| Paper type | One or more of: design, implementation, evaluation, retrospective, empirical defect study, position or analytical argument; with page | SQ1–SQ19 | all |
| System | Name of each system the paper describes or evaluates, year built, built by whom; status: design only / simulated / FPGA / silicon / running kernel / deployed commercially; with page | SQ1, SQ5, SQ6 | I1, I2, I4 |
| Levels with message semantics | For each level (hardware, microcode, instruction set, kernel, runtime or virtual machine, language): is a message send the primitive at that level, yes / partly / no / not stated (yes means every state change at that level is caused by a message send, with no other path; partly means a message is a primitive at that level but other paths exist, naming which operations are message-only); for kernels and multicomputers, answered separately between cores or nodes and within a core (traps, interrupts, system calls); whether the system started message-based at a level and later added paths that are not messages; with page | SQ1 | I1, I2 |
| Receiving unit and state ownership | What receives messages (object, actor, process, core, domain, other); whether its state can be read or written by anything other than itself, and how; with page | SQ1, SQ2, SQ7 | I1, I2, I3 |
| Message mechanism | Synchronous or asynchronous; how the receiver is named; ordering and delivery guarantees; buffering; what happens when the receiver is busy; how the receiver selects behaviour (dispatch); with page | SQ1, SQ3 | I1, I2, I3 |
| Non-message primitives | Every mechanism the paper states the system keeps that is not a message send: shared or global memory, interrupts, traps, privileged instructions, microcode, global registers, direct memory access, I/O ports, other; at which level; the reason the paper gives for keeping each; with page | SQ2 | I1, I2 |
| Self-definition | Which levels are implemented in the system's own objects and messages, and which in a lower language, microcode or hardware outside the model; whether a running program can inspect or change those levels; what remains outside the system as a base (primitives, a level that is not reflected) and what that base costs or prevents; with page | SQ2, SQ16 | I1, I2, I4 |
| Interposition | Whether a third component can be placed between sender and receiver, or between a program and conventional hardware or kernel (virtual memory, virtualisation, system call interposition, input/output memory management), without changing either (yes / no / not stated); the mechanism; at which level; its cost; with page | SQ3, SQ17 | I1, I2, I4 |
| Operating system functions | For each of protection, scheduling, resource allocation (memory, devices), naming, failure handling: how the system provides it, and whether a central component (a single kernel, master core, global table or lock) is involved, yes / no / not stated (replicated parts that must agree count as coordination); what a decentralised version costs or gives up; with page | SQ4, SQ15 | I1, I4 |
| Cost of message primitives | Measured latency or cycles of one send, one dispatch, one context or actor switch; on what hardware or simulator; with page | SQ5 | I1, I2 |
| Performance results | Each result as: metric, workload, system, baseline (name, version, configuration), value for each, unit; with page | SQ5 | I1, I2, I4 |
| Scaling | Number of cores or nodes measured, metric, result at each count, baseline; with page | SQ5 | I1, I2, I4 |
| Attributed causes | Each cause the authors give for a performance result, quoted or close-paraphrased; who states it (designers or third party); whether it is inherent to the design or due to its implementation; whether a measurement isolates it; with page | SQ5, SQ6, SQ18 | I1, I2, I4 |
| Fate and reasons | What happened to the system (commercial product, research only, abandoned, superseded, still in use) and every reason the paper gives for it; who states it (designers or third party); with page | SQ6 | I1, I2, I4 |
| Concurrency defects | Study population (programs, systems, language), number of defects, defect categories used (every kind, including deadlocks, message-protocol violations and message-order defects), counts or proportions per communication mechanism (shared memory, message passing), and defects the paper claims a design prevents by construction; with page | SQ7 | I3 |
| What shapes programs | What the paper finds determines how programs are designed and how correct they are (hardware model, language, libraries, tools, training), and the kind of evidence; with page | SQ8 | I3, I4 |
| Hardware–language trade-off | Each argued or measured cost or benefit of raising the hardware interface toward the language or specialising it (performance, cost, generality, compiler optimisation), and whether it applies to a message send as the primitive; with page | SQ9 | I2, I4 |
| Model equivalence | Which model is built on which (messages on shared memory or the reverse); which properties (encapsulation, freedom from data races, interposition) and how much performance are kept or lost; with page | SQ10 | I3, I4 |
| Model mixing | Non-message mechanisms used in actor or message programs, how often, and the reasons developers give; with page | SQ11 | I3, I4 |
| Runtime limits | Where actor or message runtimes' costs and scaling limits come from; whether the hardware's shared-memory model is named as the cause, or a software technique removes it; with page | SQ12 | I4 |
| Many-core scaling | Core counts; whether there is shared memory or coherence; how inter-core communication works; the scaling result; the limits named (power, communication, serial fraction); with page | SQ13, SQ14 | I1, I4 |
| Adoption factors | For each specialised architecture: adopted or not, and the factors the paper gives (software compatibility, ecosystem, programmability, economics, kind of workload); with page | SQ6, SQ13, SQ19 | I2, I4 |
| Quality | Answer to each of Q1–Q9 in `quality.md`, with the page that supports it | SQ1–SQ19 | all |
| Notes | Anything relevant to an SQ that no field above captures; with page | SQ1–SQ19 | all |
