# P46

## Reference
Jochen Liedtke (1996). *Toward real microkernels*. Communications of the ACM 39(9), 70–77. https://doi.org/10.1145/234215.234473. P46, round-file row R0-063, screened include under I1. Version read: publisher's typeset PDF (ACM), 8 pages. Pages cited below are the printed CACM pages 70–77 (PDF page = printed page − 69).

## Deepest pass
2

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** Position or analytical argument with a retrospective of first-generation microkernels (Mach, Chorus) and a short design description of second-generation ones (Exokernel, L4). Magazine article; its numbers are partly measurements reported from other papers ([6], [8], p. 73) and partly given without a source (Mach, Exokernel and L4 IPC/RPC, pp. 72, 74–75), with [9] and [16] named for the systems' details (p. 74); not a new evaluation (pp. 73–75).
- **Context:** First-generation microkernels Amoeba, Choices, Ra, V, Chorus, L3 and Mach (p. 71). Mach's external pager [22] (p. 71) and interrupts as IPC messages [17] (p. 72). Measurements by Chen and Bershad [6] and Condict et al. [8] (p. 73). Second-generation Exokernel [9] and L4 [16]; non-microkernel alternatives Spin [2], Synthesis [20], and loadable modules in Solaris and Linux (pp. 74–75).
- **Correctness:** The central claim is that first-generation inefficiency came from "the basic architecture of these kernels", not from inherent IPC cost, because "the hardware-inherited costs of mode and address-space switching are only 3%–7% of the measured costs" (p. 74). The argument rests on the Figure 4 breakdown and on the faster L4 and Exokernel numbers (pp. 74–75). The detailed evidence is deferred to [16] ("A detailed discussion can be found in [16]", p. 74). The author states that "There is no real-life practical experience with second-generation microkernels" (pp. 76–77).
- **Contributions:** A diagnosis of why first-generation microkernels were "inefficient and inflexible" (p. 70): IPC cost (pp. 72–74) and "the policy inside the microkernel" (p. 74). Two evaluation criteria, conservative and progressive (pp. 72–73), and a relative-RPC-overhead model (Fig. 3, p. 73). A description of L4's recursive address spaces (grant, map, demap, with mapping done by IPC) and of the user-level memory servers, pagers, drivers and Unix server built on them (pp. 75–76).
- **Clarity:** Clear and well structured, with figures and FAQ sidebars (pp. 72, 76). The measurement setups are only summarised and depend on cited papers.

## Quality
| Q | Answer | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | partly | No explicit goal or contribution list. The aim is inferred from the subtitle and the opening paragraph ("Today, we observe radically new approaches…", p. 70) and the conclusion (p. 77). |
| Q2 | partly | Some message content (8- and 512-byte arguments, p. 75; a "map message" naming a virtual address, p. 75) and the receiver learning the sender (`wait for (msg, sender)`, p. 72) are given. Receiver addressing, ordering and delivery guarantees, and busy-receiver behaviour are not stated. |
| Q3 | yes | Numbers come from running kernels: Mach and Ultrix on a DECStation 5200/200, Mach and L4 on a 486-DX50, Exokernel on a Mips R3000 (pp. 73–75). |
| Q4 | partly | Most numbers name a baseline (Mach vs Ultrix, p. 73; L4 vs Mach, p. 75; Exokernel vs Mach, p. 74). Others do not: user-level drivers "perform as well as integrated drivers" (p. 72) and "improved by an order of magnitude" (p. 77). |
| Q5 | partly | Hardware (486-DX50, DECStation 5200/200, R3000, Alpha 133 MHz) and workloads (sed, egrep, yacc, gcc, compress, ab, espresso; AIM III) are named (pp. 72–75). No reason for choosing the workloads and no number of runs. |
| Q6 | partly | The subtitle's "vastly improved" performance and the conclusion's "performance … improved by an order of magnitude" (p. 77) are backed in the body (5 µs vs 115 µs, p. 75; "up to 20 times faster", p. 75). The flexibility improvement is not quantified. |
| Q7 | partly | The IPC attribution has a breakdown (73% / 10% / 17%, p. 73) and the hardware share has Figure 4 (3%–7%, p. 74). The claims that the cause is "the basic architecture" and "step-by-step development" (pp. 74, 77) and that cache misses "are caused by the Mach kernel, invoked for IPC" (p. 73) are asserted here, or deferred to [16]. |
| Q8 | partly | The conclusion says the paper covered "only the known problems", that there is "no real-life practical experience", and that "new problems can arise" (pp. 76–77). It also leaves open questions (pp. 74–75). There is no section on threats to validity. |
| Q9 | partly | The sole author self-cites the L3 and L4 work ("In [16], we show", p. 74; refs [15], [16], [17], p. 77) and works at GMD, where L4 was "Developed" (pp. 74, 77); that he designed L3 and L4 is inferred, not stated. The Mach, Ultrix, Chorus and Exokernel numbers are reported from other authors' work ([6], [8], [9]; pp. 73–74). |

## Extracted fields
| Field | Value | Page |
|---|---|---|
| Reference | See Reference above. I1(c): the kernel's stated means of communication with and between system services is IPC. "Ideally, the kernel implements only address spaces, interprocess communication (IPC), and basic scheduling. All servers—even device drivers—run in user mode" (p. 70). "Unix system calls are implemented by IPC" (p. 76). | pp. 70, 76 |
| Paper type | Position or analytical argument; retrospective (first-generation microkernels); design (L4 address-space concept, described briefly). | pp. 70–77 |
| System | First generation: Amoeba, Choices, Ra and V (academic projects), and Chorus, L3 and Mach, which "moved to commercial use". Mach was "the flagship of industrial microkernels". Mach 3 offers "approximately 140 system calls" and needs "more than 300 Kbytes of code". Builders and years not given in the text. Status: running kernels, deployed commercially (Chorus, L3, Mach). | pp. 71, 74 |
| System | Exokernel, "developed at MIT in 1994-95", "tailored to the Mips architecture". Status: running kernel (measured RPC on R3000). | p. 74 |
| System | L4, "Developed at GMD in 1995". It has three abstractions (address spaces, threads, IPC), "implements only seven system calls, and needs only 12 Kbytes of code", and runs on a 486-DX50 with a different implementation for the Pentium. Status: running kernel, research ("second-generation microkernel design is still research"). | pp. 74–75, 77 |
| System | Also mentioned without detail: Spin (kernel-integrated compiler), Synthesis, and Solaris and Linux (kernel-loadable modules). | p. 75 |
| Levels with message semantics | Hardware and instruction set: not stated. The processors named are conventional (486-DX50, Pentium, DEC Alpha, Mips R3000, DECStation 5200/200). The only hardware costs given are kernel entry/exit and address-space switches (Fig. 4). (inferred: no message mechanism at these levels.) | pp. 72–75 |
| Levels with message semantics | Kernel, within a core: partly. IPC is the primitive between kernel and services: interrupts are delivered as messages ("The kernel captures the interrupt but does not handle it, instead generating a message"), page faults are forwarded to user-level pagers (Fig. 1), mapping pages is "implemented by IPC", Unix system calls are "implemented by IPC", and the pager-client, pager-memory server and pager-device driver interfaces "are completely based on IPC". Other paths exist: L4 has seven system calls besides IPC, and demap needs no consent ("explicit consent of the address-space owners is not required"). Drivers "read/write i/o ports" directly, and mapped pages give shared memory. | pp. 71, 72, 75, 76 |
| Levels with message semantics | Kernel, between cores or nodes: not stated. The paper's measurements are uniprocessor ("this uniprocessor", p. 73). Remote IPC goes through user-level "communication servers translating local messages to external communication protocols" (p. 76). | pp. 73, 76 |
| Levels with message semantics | Started message-based, later added non-message paths: yes, for Chorus and Mach. "both Chorus and Mach reintegrated the most critical servers and drivers into the kernel". "Chorus's 'supervisor actors' and Mach's 'kernel-loaded tasks' run in kernel mode, can freely access kernel space, and can freely interact with each other." Most first-generation kernels "implement all time-critical drivers as kernel drivers" (except L3). | pp. 72, 73 |
| Receiving unit and state ownership | Receiver: a thread in an address space (driver thread `wait for (msg, sender)`). An interrupt message goes to "the user-level process currently associated with the interrupt". "Since each server has its own address space, all these objects are protected from one another." | pp. 70, 72 |
| Receiving unit and state ownership | Access by others: the address-space owner ("the thread or threads that execute inside the address space", fn. 3) can grant or map its pages to another space if the recipient agrees. After mapping, "the page can be accessed in both address spaces". The owner can demap without the recipients' consent. A pager "can corrupt the data it maintains", and a driver whose hardware allows "physical memory access via DMA" can corrupt the system ("no kernel can prevent" it). | pp. 72, 75 |
| Message mechanism | Synchronous or asynchronous: not stated. An RPC is "two IPCs—the call and the return message", and the driver loop blocks in `wait for (msg, sender)` (inferred: blocking receive). | pp. 72 |
| Message mechanism | Naming: the receiver learns the sender, and a hardware interrupt appears as a sender ("if sender = my hardware interrupt"). How the sender names the receiver is not stated. | p. 72 |
| Message mechanism | Ordering and delivery guarantees, buffering, and busy-receiver behaviour: not stated. | — |
| Message mechanism | Content: L4 IPC is measured with 8-byte and 512-byte arguments. A map message carries a page; the mappee states, "by an appropriate receive operation", that it accepts a mapping and where (virtual address). Exokernel's "basic communication primitive is the protected control transfer that crosses address spaces but does not transfer arguments". | pp. 74, 75 |
| Message mechanism | Dispatch: the receiving thread tests the sender in its own code (`if sender = my hardware interrupt then … else …`). | p. 72 |
| Non-message primitives | Kernel: address-space operations grant, map and demap are "retained inside the kernel". Grant and map are done by IPC; demap needs no consent. Reason: "Mapping and demapping are required to implement memory managers and pagers on top of the microkernel"; "Granting is used only in special situations to avoid double bookkeeping and address-space overflow". | p. 75 |
| Non-message primitives | Shared memory: mapped pages are shared between address spaces; "The Unix server … can share memory for communication with its clients"; "Application-specific memory sharing and distributed shared memory can also be implemented by user-level servers". Reason given for the Unix server: "communication with its clients". | pp. 71, 75, 76 |
| Non-message primitives | I/O ports: included "in address spaces", and drivers "read/write i/o ports" directly. Reason: so that "interrupt handling and device I/O are done completely outside of the kernel". | p. 72 |
| Non-message primitives | DMA: named as a hardware path that can bypass encapsulation; "Risk depends on the hardware accessible to the driver". It is kept because it is a hardware fact, not a design choice (inferred). | p. 72 |
| Non-message primitives | Kernel-mode extensions in first-generation kernels: supervisor actors and kernel-loaded tasks (and loadable modules in Solaris and Linux, the Spin kernel compiler). Reason: "Gaining performance by saving user-kernel and address-space switches". | pp. 73, 75 |
| Non-message primitives | Exokernel: multiplexes "hardware primitives in a secure way", with an interface "dedicated to software-controlled translation lookalike buffers", and includes device drivers. Reason: "abstractions are costly and restrict flexibility". | p. 74 |
| Self-definition | In the kernel: address spaces, threads, IPC and (ideally) basic scheduling. Outside, at user level: servers, device drivers, pagers, memory managers, the Unix server and communication servers. The kernel's implementation language is not stated. The kernel is processor-specific: "microkernels are inherently not portable", and the 486 and the Pentium "need different microkernel implementations (with the same API)". | pp. 70, 74–76 |
| Self-definition | Change at run time: user-level drivers "can be replaced, removed, or added dynamically—without linking a new kernel and rebooting the system", and modifications "can be made and tested online". The kernel itself cannot be changed this way (not stated; inferred). Base cost: "the kernel is not usable without a memory server". | pp. 71, 72, 76 |
| Interposition | Not stated as a yes/no property. Nearest mechanisms: "Memory managers can easily be stacked", and pagers are stacked over memory servers (Fig. 6). "Remote IPC is implemented by communication servers translating local messages to external communication protocols." "Stacked address spaces … and stacked file systems … can be realized in the same fashion." The paper does not say this works without changing sender or receiver. Level: user-level servers over kernel IPC and mapping. Cost not given. | p. 76 |
| Operating system functions | Protection: one address space per server and driver. Drivers "can access only the memory and the I/O ports granted to them". The kernel is central ("It is a kernel because it is mandatory to all other levels. There is no alternative kernel"). The trusted computing base "comprises only the hardware, the microkernel, a disk driver, and perhaps a basic file system". Central component: yes (the kernel). | pp. 70–72, 76 |
| Operating system functions | Scheduling: "basic scheduling" is in the kernel. Policy and central component: not stated. | p. 70 |
| Operating system functions | Memory allocation: "An initial address space represents the physical memory and is controlled by the first address-space server". Further spaces are built recursively, and several memory servers may coexist. "Multimedia and timesharing resource allocators can coexist if the servers cooperate." Central component: yes, the initial memory server as root (inferred from the recursive construction). | pp. 75–76 |
| Operating system functions | Devices: user-level drivers with I/O ports in their address spaces, interrupts delivered as messages. Central component: the kernel, which "captures the interrupt". | p. 72 |
| Operating system functions | Naming: not stated. | — |
| Operating system functions | Failure handling: "Server malfunction is as isolated as normal application malfunction" (listed among the advantages that "seemed obvious"). A faulty driver can corrupt "any component relying on their functionality, but not the whole system". | pp. 71, 72 |
| Operating system functions | Cost of the decentralised version: user-level pagers "In principle" cost "only one IPC". First-generation pagers used "up to eight additional IPCs", with overheads of 1,000 µs. Inflexibility came from the kernel keeping memory policy ("main memory is still managed by the microkernel"). | pp. 72, 74 |
| Cost of message primitives | Mach 3 IPC: "about 115 µs per IPC on a 486-DX50" (measured; who measured is not stated). # Selection criteria

A paper is included if it meets at least one inclusion criterion and no exclusion criterion. Each verdict names the criterion that decided it. There is no restriction on publication date. "Message-based" in these criteria means: meets I1.

Terms used in the criteria and the SQs:
- **Below the programming language:** in the operating system kernel, the instruction set, microcode or hardware; not in a language runtime, library or virtual machine hosted on a conventional kernel (as in X2).
- **Written in its own objects and messages:** the level's code is objects receiving messages in the system's own model, not a lower language, microcode or hardware outside that model.
- **Without changing either:** neither the sender's nor the receiver's code, nor how they name each other, is modified to place the component between them.

| ID | Inclusion criterion |
|---|---|
| I1 | A paper is included if it describes, implements, simulates or evaluates a processor, instruction set, microarchitecture, multicomputer node or operating system kernel in which sending a message, invoking a method on an object, or delivering a message to an actor is a primitive of that level, i.e. one of: (a) an instruction of the instruction set; (b) a hardware or microcode mechanism; (c) for a kernel, the stated means by which the kernel and its system services, or the kernel's own parts, communicate (as in microkernels, multikernels, or operating systems written in an object or actor language that run without an underlying conventional kernel). The paper must name the mechanism with at least one of these terms: message, message passing, send, mailbox, actor, active message, inter-process communication (IPC), method invocation. (SQ1–SQ5) |
| I2 | A paper is included if it is a retrospective, evaluation or historical account of at least one computer architecture that its authors describe as directed at a high-level language, object-based, object-oriented or message-driven, and it reports either measured performance of that architecture or a stated reason for its performance, adoption, abandonment, or becoming unnecessary. (SQ5, SQ6) |
| I3 | A paper is included if it is an empirical study of concurrency defects (bugs) in real programs or systems (not only examples written by the authors) and it reports counts or proportions of defects either split by communication mechanism (shared memory versus message passing) or for programs or systems built on message passing only, or for programs or systems built on shared memory only, as the comparison baseline for SQ7. Programs whose defects are reported as accesses to shared variables count as shared-memory programs even if the paper does not use that term. (SQ7) |
| I4 | A paper is included if it reports evidence or an argument that directly answers one of SQ8–SQ19, whether or not it mentions messages or objects. (SQ8–SQ19) |

| ID | Exclusion criterion |
|---|---|
| X1 | A paper is excluded if it meets none of I1, I2, I3, I4. |
| X2 | A paper included only through I1 is excluded if message passing appears only at the application, library, language runtime, virtual machine or network-protocol level, running on a processor whose instruction set and hardware have no message mechanism and on a kernel that fails I1(c) (e.g. an actor library, the Erlang virtual machine, a Message Passing Interface library, a Smalltalk virtual machine hosted on Unix or Windows). Does not apply to papers that meet I2 or I3. |
| X3 | A paper is excluded if the system is a cluster or network of separate computers, each with a processor whose instruction set and hardware have no message mechanism and a kernel that fails I1(c), and the message mechanism lies only in the network interface or interconnect between them. |
| X4 | A paper is excluded if the hardware it presents is stated to serve only a fixed function or domain (e.g. neural-network inference, signal processing, packet switching, graphics) and is not stated to run general programs. Does not apply to papers included through I4. |
| X5 | A paper is excluded if it is not one of: journal article; conference or workshop paper longer than 2 pages; book or book chapter; doctoral or master's thesis; technical report of a university, company research laboratory or standards body; magazine article of a professional society (Association for Computing Machinery, Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, USENIX); architecture or system reference manual published by the system's manufacturer. Patents, slides, posters, extended abstracts of 2 pages or fewer, blog posts, forum posts, encyclopaedia entries and product brochures are excluded. |
| X6 | A paper is excluded if its full text is in neither English nor Spanish. |
| X7 | A paper is excluded if its full text cannot be obtained from the publisher, an author's or institution's web page, arXiv, Semantic Scholar, the Internet Archive, or the university library. The sources tried are recorded with the verdict. |
| X8 | A paper is excluded if it reports the same system and the same results as another included paper. The one with more pages is kept; the other is excluded unless it reports at least one measurement, design element or stated reason absent from the kept one. |
| X9 | A paper is excluded if its title or abstract presents it as a survey, review, overview or taxonomy of other work and it reports no measurement and states no reason under I2 of its own. Its reference list is still used for snowballing. |

# Agent contract

What every agent in `.claude/agents/` does, whatever its role. The agent's own file adds only its role.

From the step skill that dispatched you:
- **Row:** the flow row you run (e.g. `3a`), defined in `ai/flow-sls.md` or `ai/flow-dsrm.md`.

## Reference
Kevin Elphinstone, Gernot Heiser (2013). *From L3 to seL4: What Have We Learnt in 20 Years of L4 Microkernels?* Proceedings of the 24th ACM Symposium on Operating Systems Principles (SOSP '13), Farmington, PA, USA, pp. 133–150. https://doi.org/10.1145/2517349.2522720. Version: the proceedings version (ACM copyright block and DOI on p.133), downloaded from sigops.org (`https://www.sigops.org/s/conferences/sosp/2013/papers/p133-elphinstone.pdf`) and saved as `papers/P48.pdf`. Its 18 PDF pages carry the printed proceedings page numbers 133–150, so the offset is 132 (PDF page 1 = p.133). All pages cited below are the printed ones. The body runs pp.133–147 and the references pp.147–150.

## Deepest pass
2

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** A retrospective by two of the system's designers. It reviews 20 years of design and implementation decisions across the L4 microkernel family, from L3 to seL4, and reports which were "Retained", "Replaced", "Abandoned", "Added" or remain "Unresolved" (pp.133, 136–147). It reports a few measurements (Table 1, p.135; pp.137, 140, 146), but it is not an evaluation paper.
- **Context:** Liedtke's L4 papers [Liedtke 1993a, p.133; 1995, p.136] and the "microkernel minimality principle" (p.136); the early-1990s IPC cost problem [Condict et al. 1994; Chen and Bershad 1993] (p.133); EROS and capabilities (pp.135, 138); seL4 verification [Klein et al. 2009] (p.133) and WCET analysis [Blackham et al. 2011] (p.135); the multikernel [Baumann et al. 2009] (pp.133, 143).
- **Correctness:** The main assumption is that IPC latency counted in cycles can be compared across very different processors. The authors hedge this themselves: "as far as comparisons across vastly different ISAs and micro architectures have any validity" (p.147). Most "lessons" are argued from the authors' own experience rather than measured. The few numbers are partly taken from cited work (Warton 2005, Nourai 2005, Liedtke 1993a; pp.138, 144).
- **Contributions:** (1) A history and family tree of L4 kernels (Fig. 1, p.134; pp.133–135). (2) One-way IPC cost across eleven kernel and processor pairs from 1993 to 2013 (Table 1, p.135) and kernel sizes (Table 2, p.136). (3) A verdict on each original L4 design principle and implementation trick (Sections 3–4, pp.136–146). (4) The conclusion that "the most general principles behind L4, minimality (including running device drivers at user level) and a strong focus on performance, still remain relevant" (p.147).
- **Clarity:** Clearly written. Each subsection ends with a boxed verdict (e.g. "Abandoned: Long IPC.", p.138). The measurement method behind Table 1 is not described.

## Quality
| Q | Answer | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | yes | The abstract states the aim in one place: "we examine the lessons learnt in those 20 years about microkernel design and implementation" (p.133), and the introduction repeats it (p.133). |
| Q2 | partly | Three of the four items are described: message format (in-register and virtual message registers, long messages; p.137), naming of the receiver (thread IDs, then port-like endpoints; p.138), and the busy receiver (rendezvous blocking, timeouts, then poll/block flags; pp.136, 138–139). Delivery and ordering guarantees are not stated. |
| Q3 | yes | The systems are running kernels, several deployed commercially (pp.134–135); Table 1 reports one-way IPC on real processors (p.135). |
| Q4 | partly | Some claims name a baseline: in-register transfer vs passing via the kernel stack on ARM11 and Cortex A9 (p.137), and Warton's event kernel vs the Pistachio process kernel (p.144). Others do not: Table 1 has no baseline (p.135), and "fastest IPC we had measured on any other kernel on the same hardware" does not name the kernel (p.146). |
| Q5 | partly | Table 1 gives the processor and clock rate for each kernel (p.135), and the workload is one-way IPC. No measurement procedure, number of runs or reason for the choice of workload is reported. |
| Q6 | yes | The quantitative conclusions ("IPC latency, has remained essentially unchanged (in terms of clock cycles)" and "the code size has essentially remained constant", p.147) are reported in Table 1 (p.135) and Table 2 (p.136). The abstract makes no numeric claim. |
| Q7 | partly | Some attributed effects are measured: the benefit of in-register transfer shrinks from ARM11 to Cortex A9 (p.137), and the mapping database takes 25–50% of kernel memory (p.140). The causes of seL4's 188-cycle IPC are only asserted ("partially a result of ...", p.146). |
| Q8 | partly | There is no limitations section. Hedges appear in passing (p.147 comparability caveat; "we make no strong representations here", p.143), and the paper lists items as "Unresolved" (p.143). |
| Q9 | no | Both authors are designers of seL4, the main system examined: "we instead opted for a from-scratch implementation for our capability-based seL4 kernel" (p.135); "We base our examination ... on seL4, which we know well" (p.135). |

A block of virtual IPC message registers is shared between the kernel and user level (p.143). | pp.137–143 |

(6) **Counting semaphores** (NOVA) and **virtual IRQs** (OKL4, Fiasco.OC), with no reason stated beyond the drawbacks of synchronous-only IPC (pp.136–137). (7) **OKL4 channels**, an asynchronous bulk-transfer mechanism, "retained for compatibility" for a >50-thread application "where a separate communication page per pair of communicating threads was too costly" (p.138). Reasons: verification for the lock; scalability for RCU (p.143). (10) **User access to a timer**, which replaced timeouts for timed sleeps (p.139). Device drivers are user-level processes, except the timer and interrupt-controller drivers (p.139). The kernel itself is written in a lower language outside the message model: assembler (original L4), C/C++ (later kernels), and C for seL4 because "the requirements of verifications forced the choice of C" (pp.134, 146–147). seL4's C is "mostly a 'blind' manual translation from Haskell" (p.136 fn.4). Remaining base and its cost: the in-kernel scheduler is "the last major holdout of policy in the kernel. | Concept | What the paper says | Page |

| Asynchronous endpoint / notification (new) | A single-word notification field; a send ORs a bit mask into it, and the receiver blocks or polls; "similar to multiple binary semaphores allocated within a single word". | pp.136–137 |
| Virtual message registers (new) | A configurable set of 16–64 message registers, some physical and the rest in a pinned per-thread memory area. | p.137 |
| Long IPC (new) | Multi-buffer messages copied by the kernel through a temporary mapping window; "Abandoned" because of complexity and verification, with shared buffers used instead. | pp.137–138 |
| IPC endpoint (port-like) (new) | A kernel object that holds the queue of pending senders or receivers and is the message destination instead of a thread ID; no buffering. | p.138 |
| Clans and chiefs (new) | Kernel redirection of messages that cross a clan boundary to the clan's chief; supports confinement; "Abandoned". | p.139 |
| User-level device drivers / interrupts as IPC (new) | Drivers are user processes, and interrupts are "IPC messages, which the kernel sends to the driver"; "Retained". | p.139 |
| Recursive page mappings / mapping database (new) | Authority over frames comes from existing mappings, established through IPC (map, grant, unmap); needs a mapping database. | pp.140–141 |
| Untyped memory and retype (seL4 kernel memory model) (new) | All kernel memory is subject to capabilities; "Retyping is the only way to create objects in seL4"; capability derivation tree; called "seL4's main contribution to OS design". | pp.141–142 |
| Event-based (single-stack) kernel (new) | One kernel stack with continuations instead of one stack per thread; "Replaced: Process kernel by event kernel in seL4, OKL4 and NOVA". | p.144 |
| Lazy scheduling / Benno scheduling (new) | Lazy: blocked threads are left in the ready queue. Benno: the ready queue holds all runnable threads except the running one, which gives a bounded WCET. | pp.144–145 |
| Direct process switch (new) | On IPC the kernel switches straight to the partner thread on the caller's time slice; "a form of time-slice donation". | p.145 |
| Clustered multikernel (new) | A big-lock kernel across cores sharing an L2 cache, combined with a restricted multikernel (no memory migration between kernels). | p.143 |
| IPC fast path (new) | Hand-optimised common-case IPC code, once in assembler and in seL4 in C; it achieves 188 cycles on ARM11. | p.146 |

# Selection criteria

A paper is included if it meets at least one inclusion criterion and no exclusion criterion. Each verdict names the criterion that decided it. There is no restriction on publication date. "Message-based" in these criteria means: meets I1.

Terms used in the criteria and the SQs:
- **Below the programming language:** in the operating system kernel, the instruction set, microcode or hardware; not in a language runtime, library or virtual machine hosted on a conventional kernel (as in X2).
- **Written in its own objects and messages:** the level's code is objects receiving messages in the system's own model, not a lower language, microcode or hardware outside that model.
- **Without changing either:** neither the sender's nor the receiver's code, nor how they name each other, is modified to place the component between them.

| ID | Inclusion criterion |
|---|---|
| I1 | A paper is included if it describes, implements, simulates or evaluates a processor, instruction set, microarchitecture, multicomputer node or operating system kernel in which sending a message, invoking a method on an object, or delivering a message to an actor is a primitive of that level, i.e. one of: (a) an instruction of the instruction set; (b) a hardware or microcode mechanism; (c) for a kernel, the stated means by which the kernel and its system services, or the kernel's own parts, communicate (as in microkernels, multikernels, or operating systems written in an object or actor language that run without an underlying conventional kernel). The paper must name the mechanism with at least one of these terms: message, message passing, send, mailbox, actor, active message, inter-process communication (IPC), method invocation. (SQ1–SQ5) |
| I2 | A paper is included if it is a retrospective, evaluation or historical account of at least one computer architecture that its authors describe as directed at a high-level language, object-based, object-oriented or message-driven, and it reports either measured performance of that architecture or a stated reason for its performance, adoption, abandonment, or becoming unnecessary. (SQ5, SQ6) |
| I3 | A paper is included if it is an empirical study of concurrency defects (bugs) in real programs or systems (not only examples written by the authors) and it reports counts or proportions of defects either split by communication mechanism (shared memory versus message passing) or for programs or systems built on message passing only, or for programs or systems built on shared memory only, as the comparison baseline for SQ7. Programs whose defects are reported as accesses to shared variables count as shared-memory programs even if the paper does not use that term. (SQ7) |
| I4 | A paper is included if it reports evidence or an argument that directly answers one of SQ8–SQ19, whether or not it mentions messages or objects. (SQ8–SQ19) |

| ID | Exclusion criterion |
|---|---|
| X1 | A paper is excluded if it meets none of I1, I2, I3, I4. |
| X2 | A paper included only through I1 is excluded if message passing appears only at the application, library, language runtime, virtual machine or network-protocol level, running on a processor whose instruction set and hardware have no message mechanism and on a kernel that fails I1(c) (e.g. an actor library, the Erlang virtual machine, a Message Passing Interface library, a Smalltalk virtual machine hosted on Unix or Windows). Does not apply to papers that meet I2 or I3. |
| X3 | A paper is excluded if the system is a cluster or network of separate computers, each with a processor whose instruction set and hardware have no message mechanism and a kernel that fails I1(c), and the message mechanism lies only in the network interface or interconnect between them. |
| X4 | A paper is excluded if the hardware it presents is stated to serve only a fixed function or domain (e.g. neural-network inference, signal processing, packet switching, graphics) and is not stated to run general programs. Does not apply to papers included through I4. |
| X5 | A paper is excluded if it is not one of: journal article; conference or workshop paper longer than 2 pages; book or book chapter; doctoral or master's thesis; technical report of a university, company research laboratory or standards body; magazine article of a professional society (Association for Computing Machinery, Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, USENIX); architecture or system reference manual published by the system's manufacturer. Patents, slides, posters, extended abstracts of 2 pages or fewer, blog posts, forum posts, encyclopaedia entries and product brochures are excluded. |
| X6 | A paper is excluded if its full text is in neither English nor Spanish. |
| X7 | A paper is excluded if its full text cannot be obtained from the publisher, an author's or institution's web page, arXiv, Semantic Scholar, the Internet Archive, or the university library. The sources tried are recorded with the verdict. |
| X8 | A paper is excluded if it reports the same system and the same results as another included paper. The one with more pages is kept; the other is excluded unless it reports at least one measurement, design element or stated reason absent from the kept one. |
| X9 | A paper is excluded if its title or abstract presents it as a survey, review, overview or taxonomy of other work and it reports no measurement and states no reason under I2 of its own. Its reference list is still used for snowballing. |

# SQ8
## Question
What empirical evidence shows that the hardware's execution model, rather than the language, libraries, tools or training, determines how programmers design and write programs, and how correct those programs are?
## Why it matters to the observation
The notes' first premise ("the machine model shapes how programs are written") rests only on two Turing Award lectures, which are essays, not measurements. # Data extraction form

Fields filled for every included paper (`sls/3-reading/P*.md`). Every SQ is served by at least one field.

- **Applies to:** a field applies to papers included under the criteria in its *Applies to* column; for I4, only the fields serving the SQs the paper answers. A field that does not apply is written `n/a (I3)` (the paper's criterion). `not stated` means the field applies but the paper is silent.
- **Values:** every number in *Cost of message primitives*, *Performance results* and *Scaling* is tagged `measured`, `simulated`, `design figure`, `analytical` or `read off` (estimated from a plot).

| Field | What to record | Serves | Applies to |
|---|---|---|---|
| Reference | Authors, year, title, venue, pages; P ID; criteria that included it (I1–I4). Pages cited in the record are those printed on `papers/P*.pdf` (else its PDF page); say which version it is (publisher, preprint, manuscript, reprint), give the publisher's page range and any offset. Content taken from an abstract only cites `abstract` | SQ1–SQ19 | all |
| Paper type | One or more of: design, implementation, evaluation, retrospective, empirical defect study, position or analytical argument; with page | SQ1–SQ19 | all |
| System | Name of each system the paper describes or evaluates, year built, built by whom; status: design only / simulated / FPGA / silicon / running kernel / deployed commercially; with page | SQ1, SQ5, SQ6 | I1, I2, I4 |
| Levels with message semantics | For each level (hardware, microcode, instruction set, kernel, runtime or virtual machine, language): is a message send the primitive at that level, yes / partly / no / not stated (yes means every state change at that level is caused by a message send, with no other path; partly means a message is a primitive at that level but other paths exist, naming which operations are message-only); for kernels and multicomputers, answered separately between cores or nodes and within a core (traps, interrupts, system calls); whether the system started message-based at a level and later added paths that are not messages; with page | SQ1 | I1, I2 |
| Receiving unit and state ownership | What receives messages (object, actor, process, core, domain, other); whether its state can be read or written by anything other than itself, and how; with page | SQ1, SQ2, SQ7 | I1, I2, I3 |
| Message mechanism | Synchronous or asynchronous; how the receiver is named; ordering and delivery guarantees; buffering; what happens when the receiver is busy; how the receiver selects behaviour (dispatch); with page | SQ1, SQ3 | I1, I2, I3 |
| Non-message primitives | Every mechanism the paper states the system keeps that is not a message send: shared or global memory, interrupts, traps, privileged instructions, microcode, global registers, direct memory access, I/O ports, other; at which level; the reason the paper gives for keeping each; with page | SQ2 | I1, I2 |
| Self-definition | Which levels are implemented in the system's own objects and messages, and which in a lower language, microcode or hardware outside the model; whether a running program can inspect or change those levels; what remains outside the system as a base (primitives, a level that is not reflected) and what that base costs or prevents; with page | SQ2, SQ16 | I1, I2, I4 |
| Interposition | Whether a third component can be placed between sender and receiver, or between a program and conventional hardware or kernel (virtual memory, virtualisation, system call interposition, input/output memory management), without changing either (yes / no / not stated); the mechanism; at which level; its cost; with page | SQ3, SQ17 | I1, I2, I4 |
| Operating system functions | For each of protection, scheduling, resource allocation (memory, devices), naming, failure handling: how the system provides it, and whether a central component (a single kernel, master core, global table or lock) is involved, yes / no / not stated (replicated parts that must agree count as coordination); what a decentralised version costs or gives up; with page | SQ4, SQ15 | I1, I4 |
| Cost of message primitives | Measured latency or cycles of one send, one dispatch, one context or actor switch; on what hardware or simulator; with page | SQ5 | I1, I2 |
| Performance results | Each result as: metric, workload, system, baseline (name, version, configuration), value for each, unit; with page | SQ5 | I1, I2, I4 |
| Scaling | Number of cores or nodes measured, metric, result at each count, baseline; with page | SQ5 | I1, I2, I4 |

# P70

## Reference
Waldemar Horwat (1991). *Concurrent Smalltalk on the Message-Driven Processor*. MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, Technical Report 1321 (AITR-1321); also DTIC ADA259417. Second edition, "Updated September 26, 1991", of an S.M. thesis submitted to MIT EECS on May 12, 1989 (title and abstract pages, unnumbered, PDF pp. 3, 5). https://openalex.org/W1564741993, http://hdl.handle.net/1721.1/7090. P70, screened include under I1 (row R0-122). Pages below are the printed page numbers of the scanned report. Printed page = PDF page − 16 (checked at pp. 1, 98, 176).

## Deepest pass
2

## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** Implementation and evaluation report (a master's thesis issued as a technical report). It covers a language (Concurrent Smalltalk, CST), its compiler (Optimist II) and an operating system (Cosmos) for the Message-Driven Processor (MDP) and J-Machine. Measurements were taken on a simulator (pp. 108, 127).
- **Context:** The J-Machine and MDP [14, 16] (p. 2), built by Dally's group (p. ii). JOSS, Totty's earlier kernel, is the source of the BRAT and the object-migration protocol (p. 5). The first Optimist compiler [21] (p. 22). Related work: Smalltalk-80 and optimised Smalltalk (TS), Yokote and Tokoro's CONCURRENTSMALLTALK, and the actor languages Cantor and Acore (pp. 10–13).
- **Correctness:** Premise: "the routing time for a message sent from one end of even a large J-Machine to another is on the order of several microseconds. Operating system overhead on processing and dispatching that message of more than a few microseconds is not acceptable" (p. 2). Instruction counts are given as "rough estimates" (p. 102). They are cross-checked against runs on 4- and 16-node simulated J-Machines in MDPSim (pp. 108–109). The network-saturation limit is a first-order analytical model (p. 110).
- **Contributions:** Listed on p. 4: a redesign of CST; Optimist II (compiler and interpreter); Cosmos; CST runtime libraries; changes to MDPSim; "Modifications to the MDP architecture that make it more suitable for Concurrent Smalltalk." Measured results: a grain size of about 60 instructions, about 100–120 instructions per function call, and about 2 (internal memory) or about 4 (external DRAM) cycles per instruction (pp. 114, 127–128).
- **Clarity:** Clear and well structured, with message-format figures and per-routine instruction-count tables (Figs. 4-10 to 4-21, Tables 7-1 to 7-6). The scan is image-only, with no text layer. Appendix E (the compiler listing) was removed for space (p. 184).

A delivery guarantee is not stated, and queue overflow is not handled (pp. 1, 120). |

| new: grain size | "the average amount of time a method executes before suspending", measured at about 60 instructions, which the author found "surprising; it was expected to be much lower". | abstract (PDF p. 5), p. 7 |

I2 does not require silicon. No exclusion criterion found. X5: a university technical report and master's thesis. X8: this is not the same system and results as P71 (the 1988 Optimist compiler report) or P12; the overlap with P12 is limited to describing COSMOS and CST.

# SQ8

## Question
What empirical evidence shows that the hardware's execution model, rather than the language, libraries, tools or training, determines how programmers design and write programs, and how correct those programs are?

# SQ10

## Question
What does the literature report about the equivalence (duality) of message-passing and shared-memory system structures, and can either one be built on top of the other while keeping its properties (encapsulation, freedom from data races, interposition) and its performance?

## Why it matters to the observation
Lauer and Needham (1978/1979, *On the Duality of Operating System Structures*) argue that message-oriented and procedure-oriented systems are duals: a problem solved in one has a dual solution in the other. If the two are equivalent, the observation's gap may be a matter of which layer exposes which model, and putting messages in hardware may add nothing that a layer above cannot give.

# SQ11

## Question
Why do developers of actor or message-passing programs also use shared state, locks or other concurrency mechanisms alongside messages, and what do they report that the pure message model cannot express or costs too much?

## Why it matters to the observation
The observation wants a system with no escape routes from its own rules. # SQ14

## Question
What evidence shows that hardware shared memory, cache coherence and shared-memory operating system kernels scale to many cores, and what limits do studies report on the scaling of many-core hardware in general (power, communication, serial fractions)?

# SQ15

## Question
Which system functions (resource allocation, scheduling, naming, protection, failure handling, global consistency) have been shown to require global agreement or to work better with central or logically central coordination, and what do decentralised versions cost or give up?

## Why it matters to the observation
The notes want to remove the middle layer entirely. Agreement among message-passing parts has proven limits (Fischer, Lynch and Paterson, 1985, *Impossibility of Distributed Consensus with One Faulty Process*, JACM), and networking, the notes' own model, moved towards logically centralised control with software-defined networking (Kreutz et al., 2015, Proceedings of the IEEE). If key operating system functions need a coordinator, "no central coordinator" is a constraint that may make RQ5's answer "no" by construction.

# SQ16

## Question
What do studies of reflective and metacircular systems report about whether a system can be defined entirely in its own terms, what must remain outside it as a base (primitives, a level that is not reflected), and what that base costs or prevents?

## Why it matters to the observation
The observation says a system with escape routes "cannot define itself" and "cannot be taken seriously". Smith's reflective tower (1984, *Reflection and Semantics in Lisp*, POPL) is, at least virtually, an infinite stack of levels, and Squeak's virtual machine is written in Smalltalk but translated to C to run (Ingalls et al., 1997, OOPSLA). If every self-defining system needs a base that is not defined in itself, the gap may be unavoidable and the goal has to be restated as moving the base, not removing it.

# SQ18

## Question
What costs of object-based and capability-based hardware do independent evaluations attribute to object orientation, fine-grained protection or object addressing themselves, rather than to compilers or implementation, and how large are those costs?

## Why it matters to the observation

An earlier independent evaluation (Hansen et al., 1982, *A Performance Evaluation of the Intel iAPX 432*) and modern capability hardware (Woodruff et al., 2014, *The CHERI Capability Model*, ISCA) measure the cost from other angles. H2 holds only if the inherent part is small across sources, not in one.

# SQ19

## Question
Since the end of Dennard scaling, which kinds of specialised architectures have been adopted and which have failed, and what factors (software compatibility, ecosystem, programmability, economics, kind of workload) do analyses give for the difference?

## Why it matters to the observation

The specialisation that succeeded may be narrow and data-parallel (for example the tensor processing unit, Jouppi et al., 2018, CACM), far from general-purpose actor machines, and the barriers that sank earlier machines (software compatibility, ecosystem) may not have changed. SQ6 looks at the past decline; this question checks whether the present actually differs.

What empirical evidence shows that the hardware's execution model, rather than the language, libraries, tools or training, determines how programmers design and write programs, and how correct those programs are?

## Why it matters to the observation
The notes' first premise ("the machine model shapes how programs are written") rests only on two Turing Award lectures, which are essays, not measurements. If the evidence says the language or the runtime decides how people write programs, then changing the hardware does not change the programs on top of it, and the motivation needs another basis.

# SQ9

## Question
What evidence and arguments show that narrowing the semantic gap by raising the hardware interface towards the language harms performance, cost, generality or compiler optimisation, and do those arguments apply to a message send as the machine's primitive?

## Why it matters to the observation
The notes treat the semantic gap as a defect to close. The reduced instruction set argument (Patterson and Ditzel, 1980, *The Case for the Reduced Instruction Set Computer*) was made against exactly that goal. If its reasoning carries over to message sends, the observation describes a deliberate trade-off, not an oversight.

# SQ10

## Question
What does the literature report about the equivalence (duality) of message-passing and shared-memory system structures, and can either one be built on top of the other while keeping its properties (encapsulation, freedom from data races, interposition) and its performance?

## Why it matters to the observation
Lauer and Needham (1978/1979, *On the Duality of Operating System Structures*) argue that message-oriented and procedure-oriented systems are duals: a problem solved in one has a dual solution in the other. If the two are equivalent, the observation's gap may be a matter of which layer exposes which model, and putting messages in hardware may add nothing that a layer above cannot give.

# SQ11

## Question
Why do developers of actor or message-passing programs also use shared state, locks or other concurrency mechanisms alongside messages, and what do they report that the pure message model cannot express or costs too much?

## Why it matters to the observation
The observation wants a system with no escape routes from its own rules. Tasharofi, Dinges and Johnson (2013, *Why Do Scala Developers Mix the Actor Model with other Concurrency Models?*, ECOOP) report that most of the large actor programs they studied mix actors with other concurrency models, partly because of shortcomings of the actor model itself. If programmers keep building escape routes where they have the choice, a machine that removes them may be unusable rather than cleaner.

# SQ14

## Question
What evidence shows that hardware shared memory, cache coherence and shared-memory operating system kernels scale to many cores, and what limits do studies report on the scaling of many-core hardware in general (power, communication, serial fractions)?

## Why it matters to the observation
The notes say shared memory "has become a scaling cost" and that independent actors map onto many cores. # SQ15

## Question
Which system functions (resource allocation, scheduling, naming, protection, failure handling, global consistency) have been shown to require global agreement or to work better with central or logically central coordination, and what do decentralised versions cost or give up?

## Why it matters to the observation
The notes want to remove the middle layer entirely. Agreement among message-passing parts has proven limits (Fischer, Lynch and Paterson, 1985, *Impossibility of Distributed Consensus with One Faulty Process*, JACM), and networking, the notes' own model, moved towards logically centralised control with software-defined networking (Kreutz et al., 2015, Proceedings of the IEEE). If key operating system functions need a coordinator, "no central coordinator" is a constraint that may make RQ5's answer "no" by construction.

# SQ16

## Question
What do studies of reflective and metacircular systems report about whether a system can be defined entirely in its own terms, what must remain outside it as a base (primitives, a level that is not reflected), and what that base costs or prevents?

## Why it matters to the observation
The observation says a system with escape routes "cannot define itself" and "cannot be taken seriously". Smith's reflective tower (1984, *Reflection and Semantics in Lisp*, POPL) is, at least virtually, an infinite stack of levels, and Squeak's virtual machine is written in Smalltalk but translated to C to run (Ingalls et al., 1997, OOPSLA). If every self-defining system needs a base that is not defined in itself, the gap may be unavoidable and the goal has to be restated as moving the base, not removing it.

# SQ17

## Question
Which mechanisms let a layer be put between a program and conventional shared-memory hardware or kernels without changing either (virtual memory, trap-and-emulate virtualisation, system call interposition, input/output memory management), and how do their coverage and cost compare with interposition on messages?

## Why it matters to the observation
The observation says that at the low level "layers cannot be put in between the way the network allows". Virtualisation is such a layer: Popek and Goldberg (1974, *Formal Requirements for Virtualizable Third Generation Architectures*, CACM) give the conditions under which a monitor can intercept every sensitive instruction. # SQ18

## Question
What costs of object-based and capability-based hardware do independent evaluations attribute to object orientation, fine-grained protection or object addressing themselves, rather than to compilers or implementation, and how large are those costs?

## Why it matters to the observation
H2 (the 432's losses were avoidable) rests on one paper by the 432's own evaluators, and the same paper still names a residual 1–4 times slowdown as the inherent cost of the 432's style [notes, citing Colwell et al. 1988, pp. 336–337]. An earlier independent evaluation (Hansen et al., 1982, *A Performance Evaluation of the Intel iAPX 432*) and modern capability hardware (Woodruff et al., 2014, *The CHERI Capability Model*, ISCA) measure the cost from other angles. H2 holds only if the inherent part is small across sources, not in one.

Second edition, "Updated September 26, 1991", of an S.M. thesis submitted to MIT EECS on May 12, 1989 (title and abstract pages, unnumbered, PDF pp. 3, 5). https://openalex.org/W1564741993, http://hdl.handle.net/1721.1/7090. ## First pass: the five Cs
- **Category:** Implementation and evaluation report (a master's thesis issued as a technical report). It covers a language (Concurrent Smalltalk, CST), its compiler (Optimist II) and an operating system (Cosmos) for the Message-Driven Processor (MDP) and J-Machine. Measurements were taken on a simulator (pp. 108, 127).
- **Context:** The J-Machine and MDP [14, 16] (p. 2), built by Dally's group (p. ii). JOSS, Totty's earlier kernel, is the source of the BRAT and the object-migration protocol (p. 5). The first Optimist compiler [21] (p. 22). Related work: Smalltalk-80 and optimised Smalltalk (TS), Yokote and Tokoro's CONCURRENTSMALLTALK, and the actor languages Cantor and Acore (pp. 10–13).
- **Correctness:** Premise: "the routing time for a message sent from one end of even a large J-Machine to another is on the order of several microseconds. Operating system overhead on processing and dispatching that message of more than a few microseconds is not acceptable" (p. 2). Instruction counts are given as "rough estimates" (p. 102). They are cross-checked against runs on 4- and 16-node simulated J-Machines in MDPSim (pp. 108–109). The network-saturation limit is a first-order analytical model (p. 110).
- **Contributions:** Listed on p. 4: a redesign of CST; Optimist II (compiler and interpreter); Cosmos; CST runtime libraries; changes to MDPSim; "Modifications to the MDP architecture that make it more suitable for Concurrent Smalltalk." Measured results: a grain size of about 60 instructions, about 100–120 instructions per function call, and about 2 (internal memory) or about 4 (external DRAM) cycles per instruction (pp. 114, 127–128).
- **Clarity:** Clear and well structured, with message-format figures and per-routine instruction-count tables (Figs. 4-10 to 4-21, Tables 7-1 to 7-6). The scan is image-only, with no text layer. Appendix E (the compiler listing) was removed for space (p. 184).

## Question
What does the literature report about the equivalence (duality) of message-passing and shared-memory system structures, and can either one be built on top of the other while keeping its properties (encapsulation, freedom from data races, interposition) and its performance?

Lauer and Needham (1978/1979, *On the Duality of Operating System Structures*) argue that message-oriented and procedure-oriented systems are duals: a problem solved in one has a dual solution in the other. If the two are equivalent, the observation's gap may be a matter of which layer exposes which model, and putting messages in hardware may add nothing that a layer above cannot give.

# Selection criteria

A paper is included if it meets at least one inclusion criterion and no exclusion criterion. Each verdict names the criterion that decided it. There is no restriction on publication date. "Message-based" in these criteria means: meets I1.

Terms used in the criteria and the SQs:
- **Below the programming language:** in the operating system kernel, the instruction set, microcode or hardware; not in a language runtime, library or virtual machine hosted on a conventional kernel (as in X2).
- **Written in its own objects and messages:** the level's code is objects receiving messages in the system's own model, not a lower language, microcode or hardware outside that model.
- **Without changing either:** neither the sender's nor the receiver's code, nor how they name each other, is modified to place the component between them.

| ID | Inclusion criterion |
|---|---|
| I1 | A paper is included if it describes, implements, simulates or evaluates a processor, instruction set, microarchitecture, multicomputer node or operating system kernel in which sending a message, invoking a method on an object, or delivering a message to an actor is a primitive of that level, i.e. one of: (a) an instruction of the instruction set; (b) a hardware or microcode mechanism; (c) for a kernel, the stated means by which the kernel and its system services, or the kernel's own parts, communicate (as in microkernels, multikernels, or operating systems written in an object or actor language that run without an underlying conventional kernel). The paper must name the mechanism with at least one of these terms: message, message passing, send, mailbox, actor, active message, inter-process communication (IPC), method invocation. (SQ1–SQ5) |
| I2 | A paper is included if it is a retrospective, evaluation or historical account of at least one computer architecture that its authors describe as directed at a high-level language, object-based, object-oriented or message-driven, and it reports either measured performance of that architecture or a stated reason for its performance, adoption, abandonment, or becoming unnecessary. (SQ5, SQ6) |
| I3 | A paper is included if it is an empirical study of concurrency defects (bugs) in real programs or systems (not only examples written by the authors) and it reports counts or proportions of defects either split by communication mechanism (shared memory versus message passing) or for programs or systems built on message passing only, or for programs or systems built on shared memory only, as the comparison baseline for SQ7. Programs whose defects are reported as accesses to shared variables count as shared-memory programs even if the paper does not use that term. (SQ7) |
| I4 | A paper is included if it reports evidence or an argument that directly answers one of SQ8–SQ19, whether or not it mentions messages or objects. (SQ8–SQ19) |

| ID | Exclusion criterion |
|---|---|
| X1 | A paper is excluded if it meets none of I1, I2, I3, I4. |
| X2 | A paper included only through I1 is excluded if message passing appears only at the application, library, language runtime, virtual machine or network-protocol level, running on a processor whose instruction set and hardware have no message mechanism and on a kernel that fails I1(c) (e.g. an actor library, the Erlang virtual machine, a Message Passing Interface library, a Smalltalk virtual machine hosted on Unix or Windows). Does not apply to papers that meet I2 or I3. |
| X3 | A paper is excluded if the system is a cluster or network of separate computers, each with a processor whose instruction set and hardware have no message mechanism and a kernel that fails I1(c), and the message mechanism lies only in the network interface or interconnect between them. |
| X4 | A paper is excluded if the hardware it presents is stated to serve only a fixed function or domain (e.g. neural-network inference, signal processing, packet switching, graphics) and is not stated to run general programs. Does not apply to papers included through I4. |
| X5 | A paper is excluded if it is not one of: journal article; conference or workshop paper longer than 2 pages; book or book chapter; doctoral or master's thesis; technical report of a university, company research laboratory or standards body; magazine article of a professional society (Association for Computing Machinery, Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, USENIX); architecture or system reference manual published by the system's manufacturer. Patents, slides, posters, extended abstracts of 2 pages or fewer, blog posts, forum posts, encyclopaedia entries and product brochures are excluded. |
| X6 | A paper is excluded if its full text is in neither English nor Spanish. |
| X7 | A paper is excluded if its full text cannot be obtained from the publisher, an author's or institution's web page, arXiv, Semantic Scholar, the Internet Archive, or the university library. The sources tried are recorded with the verdict. |
| X8 | A paper is excluded if it reports the same system and the same results as another included paper. The one with more pages is kept; the other is excluded unless it reports at least one measurement, design element or stated reason absent from the kept one. |
| X9 | A paper is excluded if its title or abstract presents it as a survey, review, overview or taxonomy of other work and it reports no measurement and states no reason under I2 of its own. Its reference list is still used for snowballing. |

# SQ8

## Question
What empirical evidence shows that the hardware's execution model, rather than the language, libraries, tools or training, determines how programmers design and write programs, and how correct those programs are?

# SQ10

## Question
What does the literature report about the equivalence (duality) of message-passing and shared-memory system structures, and can either one be built on top of the other while keeping its properties (encapsulation, freedom from data races, interposition) and its performance?

## Why it matters to the observation
Lauer and Needham (1978/1979, *On the Duality of Operating System Structures*) argue that message-oriented and procedure-oriented systems are duals: a problem solved in one has a dual solution in the other. If the two are equivalent, the observation's gap may be a matter of which layer exposes which model, and putting messages in hardware may add nothing that a layer above cannot give.

# SQ11

## Question
Why do developers of actor or message-passing programs also use shared state, locks or other concurrency mechanisms alongside messages, and what do they report that the pure message model cannot express or costs too much?

## Why it matters to the observation
The observation wants a system with no escape routes from its own rules. Tasharofi, Dinges and Johnson (2013, *Why Do Scala Developers Mix the Actor Model with other Concurrency Models?*, ECOOP) report that most of the large actor programs they studied mix actors with other concurrency models, partly because of shortcomings of the actor model itself. # Data extraction form

Fields filled for every included paper (`sls/3-reading/P*.md`). Every SQ is served by at least one field.

- **Applies to:** a field applies to papers included under the criteria in its *Applies to* column; for I4, only the fields serving the SQs the paper answers. A field that does not apply is written `n/a (I3)` (the paper's criterion). `not stated` means the field applies but the paper is silent.
- **Values:** every number in *Cost of message primitives*, *Performance results* and *Scaling* is tagged `measured`, `simulated`, `design figure`, `analytical` or `read off` (estimated from a plot).

| Field | What to record | Serves | Applies to |
|---|---|---|---|
| Reference | Authors, year, title, venue, pages; P ID; criteria that included it (I1–I4). Pages cited in the record are those printed on `papers/P*.pdf` (else its PDF page); say which version it is (publisher, preprint, manuscript, reprint), give the publisher's page range and any offset. Content taken from an abstract only cites `abstract` | SQ1–SQ19 | all |
| Paper type | One or more of: design, implementation, evaluation, retrospective, empirical defect study, position or analytical argument; with page | SQ1–SQ19 | all |
| System | Name of each system the paper describes or evaluates, year built, built by whom; status: design only / simulated / FPGA / silicon / running kernel / deployed commercially; with page | SQ1, SQ5, SQ6 | I1, I2, I4 |
| Levels with message semantics | For each level (hardware, microcode, instruction set, kernel, runtime or virtual machine, language): is a message send the primitive at that level, yes / partly / no / not stated (yes means every state change at that level is caused by a message send, with no other path; partly means a message is a primitive at that level but other paths exist, naming which operations are message-only); for kernels and multicomputers, answered separately between cores or nodes and within a core (traps, interrupts, system calls); whether the system started message-based at a level and later added paths that are not messages; with page | SQ1 | I1, I2 |
| Receiving unit and state ownership | What receives messages (object, actor, process, core, domain, other); whether its state can be read or written by anything other than itself, and how; with page | SQ1, SQ2, SQ7 | I1, I2, I3 |
| Message mechanism | Synchronous or asynchronous; how the receiver is named; ordering and delivery guarantees; buffering; what happens when the receiver is busy; how the receiver selects behaviour (dispatch); with page | SQ1, SQ3 | I1, I2, I3 |
| Non-message primitives | Every mechanism the paper states the system keeps that is not a message send: shared or global memory, interrupts, traps, privileged instructions, microcode, global registers, direct memory access, I/O ports, other; at which level; the reason the paper gives for keeping each; with page | SQ2 | I1, I2 |
| Self-definition | Which levels are implemented in the system's own objects and messages, and which in a lower language, microcode or hardware outside the model; whether a running program can inspect or change those levels; what remains outside the system as a base (primitives, a level that is not reflected) and what that base costs or prevents; with page | SQ2, SQ16 | I1, I2, I4 |
| Interposition | Whether a third component can be placed between sender and receiver, or between a program and conventional hardware or kernel (virtual memory, virtualisation, system call interposition, input/output memory management), without changing either (yes / no / not stated); the mechanism; at which level; its cost; with page | SQ3, SQ17 | I1, I2, I4 |
| Operating system functions | For each of protection, scheduling, resource allocation (memory, devices), naming, failure handling: how the system provides it, and whether a central component (a single kernel, master core, global table or lock) is involved, yes / no / not stated (replicated parts that must agree count as coordination); what a decentralised version costs or gives up; with page | SQ4, SQ15 | I1, I4 |
| Cost of message primitives | Measured latency or cycles of one send, one dispatch, one context or actor switch; on what hardware or simulator; with page | SQ5 | I1, I2 |
| Performance results | Each result as: metric, workload, system, baseline (name, version, configuration), value for each, unit; with page | SQ5 | I1, I2, I4 |
| Scaling | Number of cores or nodes measured, metric, result at each count, baseline; with page | SQ5 | I1, I2, I4 |
| Attributed causes | Each cause the authors give for a performance result, quoted or close-paraphrased; who states it (designers or third party); whether it is inherent to the design or due to its implementation; whether a measurement isolates it; with page | SQ5, SQ6, SQ18 | I1, I2, I4 |
| Fate and reasons | What happened to the system (commercial product, research only, abandoned, superseded, still in use) and every reason the paper gives for it; who states it (designers or third party); with page | SQ6 | I1, I2, I4 |
| Concurrency defects | Study population (programs, systems, language), number of defects, defect categories used (every kind, including deadlocks, message-protocol violations and message-order defects), counts or proportions per communication mechanism (shared memory, message passing), and defects the paper claims a design prevents by construction; with page | SQ7 | I3 |
| What shapes programs | What the paper finds determines how programs are designed and how correct they are (hardware model, language, libraries, tools, training), and the kind of evidence; with page | SQ8 | I3, I4 |
| Hardware–language trade-off | Each argued or measured cost or benefit of raising the hardware interface toward the language or specialising it (performance, cost, generality, compiler optimisation), and whether it applies to a message send as the primitive; with page | SQ9 | I2, I4 |
| Model equivalence | Which model is built on which (messages on shared memory or the reverse); which properties (encapsulation, freedom from data races, interposition) and how much performance are kept or lost; with page | SQ10 | I3, I4 |
| Model mixing | Non-message mechanisms used in actor or message programs, how often, and the reasons developers give; with page | SQ11 | I3, I4 |
| Runtime limits | Where actor or message runtimes' costs and scaling limits come from; whether the hardware's shared-memory model is named as the cause, or a software technique removes it; with page | SQ12 | I4 |

| Adoption factors | For each specialised architecture: adopted or not, and the factors the paper gives (software compatibility, ecosystem, programmability, economics, kind of workload); with page | SQ6, SQ13, SQ19 | I2, I4 |
| Quality | Answer to each of Q1–Q9 in `quality.md`, with the page that supports it | SQ1–SQ19 | all |
| Notes | Anything relevant to an SQ that no field above captures; with page | SQ1–SQ19 | all |

# Quality assessment checklist

`n/a` is used only when the source was not read (abstract-only record) or the question cannot apply to the paper's kind, and always with the reason. `no` means the paper fails the question.

| ID | Question asked of each paper | Scale |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | Does the paper state its aim or contribution explicitly (in the abstract or introduction)? yes: stated in one place as a goal or contribution list; partly: has to be inferred from several places; no: not stated. | yes / partly / no / n/a |
| Q2 | Is the system's communication mechanism described in enough detail to reimplement it: message format, naming or addressing of the receiver, delivery and ordering guarantees, and what happens when the receiver is busy? yes: all four; partly: one to three; no: none. For papers with no system (I3 studies), the studied programs and their communication mechanisms count instead. | yes / partly / no / n/a |
| Q3 | Does the evidence come from a working artefact? yes: silicon, FPGA, or a kernel or system that runs real programs; partly: simulator or emulator; no: design or argument only. For I3 studies: yes: defects taken from real bug trackers or commit histories; partly: from benchmark suites; no: from examples only. Analytical models count as no (design or argument). | yes / partly / no / n/a |
| Q4 | Is every performance or defect claim measured against a named baseline? yes: each claim names its baseline (system, version, configuration); partly: some claims do; no: none do, or no measured claim is made. A hypothetical baseline counts as partly. For I3 studies: yes if the counts are compared with another named study or population; partly if only some are. | yes / partly / no / n/a |
| Q5 | Is the measurement setup reported: workloads or programs used and why they were chosen, hardware or simulator configuration, number of runs or sample size? yes: all three; partly: one or two; no: none, or nothing measured. For I3 studies: the sampling procedure (sources, search terms, screening) replaces the hardware or simulator configuration. | yes / partly / no / n/a |
| Q6 | Does every quantitative claim in the abstract and conclusions have a table, figure or text passage in the body that reports it? yes: all; partly: some; no: none, or no data in the body. | yes / partly / no / n/a |
| Q7 | Are causes attributed to results (e.g. "the slowdown comes from X") supported by a measurement that isolates that cause, such as an ablation or a breakdown? yes: every attributed cause; partly: some; no: none, or causes only asserted. | yes / partly / no / n/a |
| Q8 | Does the paper discuss limitations or threats to validity? yes: a section or paragraph dedicated to them; partly: mentioned in passing; no: not discussed. | yes / partly / no / n/a |
| Q9 | Is the evaluation independent of the system's designers? yes: no author is listed as a designer or builder of the evaluated system in the paper or its cited design papers; partly: some authors are; no: all authors are, or the paper does not evaluate a system. For I3 studies: yes if no author developed the studied programs. | yes / partly / no / n/a |

# SQ8

## Question
What empirical evidence shows that the hardware's execution model, rather than the language, libraries, tools or training, determines how programmers design and write programs, and how correct those programs are?

## Why it matters to the observation
The notes' first premise ("the machine model shapes how programs are written") rests only on two Turing Award lectures, which are essays, not measurements. If the evidence says the language or the runtime decides how people write programs, then changing the hardware does not change the programs on top of it, and the motivation needs another basis.

# SQ9

## Question
What evidence and arguments show that narrowing the semantic gap by raising the hardware interface towards the language harms performance, cost, generality or compiler optimisation, and do those arguments apply to a message send as the machine's primitive?

# SQ10

## Question
What does the literature report about the equivalence (duality) of message-passing and shared-memory system structures, and can either one be built on top of the other while keeping its properties (encapsulation, freedom from data races, interposition) and its performance?

## Why it matters to the observation
Lauer and Needham (1978/1979, *On the Duality of Operating System Structures*) argue that message-oriented and procedure-oriented systems are duals: a problem solved in one has a dual solution in the other. If the two are equivalent, the observation's gap may be a matter of which layer exposes which model, and putting messages in hardware may add nothing that a layer above cannot give.

# SQ11

## Question
Why do developers of actor or message-passing programs also use shared state, locks or other concurrency mechanisms alongside messages, and what do they report that the pure message model cannot express or costs too much?

## Why it matters to the observation
The observation wants a system with no escape routes from its own rules. Tasharofi, Dinges and Johnson (2013, *Why Do Scala Developers Mix the Actor Model with other Concurrency Models?*, ECOOP) report that most of the large actor programs they studied mix actors with other concurrency models, partly because of shortcomings of the actor model itself. If programmers keep building escape routes where they have the choice, a machine that removes them may be unusable rather than cleaner.

# SQ14

## Question
What evidence shows that hardware shared memory, cache coherence and shared-memory operating system kernels scale to many cores, and what limits do studies report on the scaling of many-core hardware in general (power, communication, serial fractions)?

# SQ15

## Question
Which system functions (resource allocation, scheduling, naming, protection, failure handling, global consistency) have been shown to require global agreement or to work better with central or logically central coordination, and what do decentralised versions cost or give up?

## Why it matters to the observation
The notes want to remove the middle layer entirely. Agreement among message-passing parts has proven limits (Fischer, Lynch and Paterson, 1985, *Impossibility of Distributed Consensus with One Faulty Process*, JACM), and networking, the notes' own model, moved towards logically centralised control with software-defined networking (Kreutz et al., 2015, Proceedings of the IEEE). If key operating system functions need a coordinator, "no central coordinator" is a constraint that may make RQ5's answer "no" by construction.

# SQ16

## Question
What do studies of reflective and metacircular systems report about whether a system can be defined entirely in its own terms, what must remain outside it as a base (primitives, a level that is not reflected), and what that base costs or prevents?

## Why it matters to the observation
The observation says a system with escape routes "cannot define itself" and "cannot be taken seriously". Smith's reflective tower (1984, *Reflection and Semantics in Lisp*, POPL) is, at least virtually, an infinite stack of levels, and Squeak's virtual machine is written in Smalltalk but translated to C to run (Ingalls et al., 1997, OOPSLA). If every self-defining system needs a base that is not defined in itself, the gap may be unavoidable and the goal has to be restated as moving the base, not removing it.
