1. Introduction

     The goal of the Smailtalk On A RISC (SOAR) project at U.C. Berkeley was to
produce a high-performance execution engine for the Smalltalk-80 1 language [1]. The
heart of the effort is a Berkeley RISC processor extended to support Smalltalk [2]. The
processor was designed in conjunction with the runtime system [3], which together
have yielded substantial performance improvements over conventional Smalltalk-80
implementations. An extensive performance evaluation can be found in Ungar's disser-
tation [4]; SOAR runs Smalltalk roughly 2.5 times as fast as a Motorola 68010 with a
similar cycle time, which works out to be about the same speed as the Xerox Dorado
high-performance workstation. One reason for the SOAR system's speed is its compila-
tion of Smalltalk, It has been estimated that compiling Smalltalk to the SOAR
instruction set produces a factor of two speedup over conventional interpreted sys-
tems. This paper describes the SOAR compiler, presenting the mechanisms of compil-
ing Smalltalk to the special-purpose SOAR RISC instruction set.                            "

2. The Nature of the Compiler

     The Smalltalk-80 language is defined operationally in terms of a virtual machine
that executes stack-based instructions called bytecodes. The Smalltalk-80 program-
ming environment is a binary image that runs on the virtual machine. The problem
with the virtual machine is that it is inefficient if naively implemented.   It is com-
monly realized as a bytecode interpreter, which requires special hardware (such as that
possessed by the Dorado) to avoid interposing a layer of overhead between the virtual
machine and the native machine.

To recapitulate: Lisp is an excellent laboratory for language experimentation for two reasons.
First, one can choose a very small subset, with only a dozen primitives or so, that is still recognizably
a member of the class of Lisp-like languages. It is very easy to bootstrap such a small language, with
variations of choice, on a new platform. If it looks promising, one can ﬂesh out the long laundry
list of amenities later. Second, it is particularly easy—the work of an hour or less—to bootstrap
such a new dialect within an existing Lisp implementation. Even if the host implementation diﬀers
in fundamental ways from the new dialect, it can provide primitive operations such as arithmetic
and I/O as well as being a programming language that is just plain convenient for writing language
interpreters. If you can live with the generic, list-structure-oriented syntax, you can have a ﬁeld
day reprogramming the semantics. After you get that right there is time enough to re-engineer it
and, if you must, slap a parser on the front.

complex history than languages with wider usage. It would seem that almost every little research
group has its own version of Lisp, and there would appear to be as many Lisps as variations on
language concepts. It is natural to ask what is so special or diﬀerent about Lisp that explains it.
There are ﬁve basic reasons: its theoretical foundations, its malleability, its interactive and

# SQ15

## Question
Which system functions (resource allocation, scheduling, naming, protection, failure handling, global consistency) have been shown to require global agreement or to work better with central or logically central coordination, and what do decentralised versions cost or give up?

## Why it matters to the observation
The notes want to remove the middle layer entirely. Agreement among message-passing parts has proven limits (Fischer, Lynch and Paterson, 1985, *Impossibility of Distributed Consensus with One Faulty Process*, JACM), and networking, the notes' own model, moved towards logically centralised control with software-defined networking (Kreutz et al., 2015, Proceedings of the IEEE). If key operating system functions need a coordinator, "no central coordinator" is a constraint that may make RQ5's answer "no" by construction.

## Question

Since the end of Dennard scaling, which kinds of specialised architectures have been adopted and which have failed, and what factors (software compatibility, ecosystem, programmability, economics, kind of workload) do analyses give for the difference?
## Why it matters to the observation
H1 says the end of free single-processor speedups reopens room for specialised machines. The specialisation that succeeded may be narrow and data-parallel (for example the tensor processing unit, Jouppi et al., 2018, CACM), far from general-purpose actor machines, and the barriers that sank earlier machines (software compatibility, ecosystem) may not have changed. SQ6 looks at the past decline; this question checks whether the present actually differs.

I checked the claims the follow-up pass changed in P261.md against the paper: 17 found, 1 differs, 0 not found. The one mismatch is a quote attributed to the wrong subject: the paper calls the virtual machine, not the bytecodes, "the semantic definition of the language".

**File written:** `/home/garro/dev/faculty/Thesis/research/sls/3-reading/P261.citations.md`, revised in place.
- All existing rows are kept as they were.
- Frontmatter is now `status: proposed`, and the diff path is added to `inputs`.
- A new section "## Follow-up pass (2026-10-13)" has 16 rows covering the 18 claims. Some rows hold more than one claim: the two Windows-and-spills quotes from p. 6 share a row, and so do the Reference section and the Reference row. All quotes were checked against the page images (printed pp. 2–4, 6–8, 10–11).
- *Suggested fixes* now holds only the fix for the new claim. It also says that the three earlier fixes were applied at gate 3c, and the revised record does carry their wording.

**Found (17):**
- The criterion statement "I4 proposed: SQ9 (pp. 3–4, 6–7, 10)", in both the Reference section and the Reference row. Each cited page has text weighing the hardware against doing the same work in the compiler.
- Two quotes on p. 6: "Register windows and spills complicate the compiler" and "SOAR architectural support for Smalltalk has in the main simplified it".
- The p. 7 quote about pointers to activation records being "not as severe a problem as it was initially feared to be".
- The claim that limits on optimisation come from the language and its bytecodes, not the hardware (pp. 3, 7; p. 10 also supports it).
- The p. 3 quote that bytecodes "restrict the compiler writer".
- The p. 7 quote "Both language and pragmatic considerations limited the optimizations we could perform".
- The p. 3 quote about window size on the chip.
- The scope note that the figures come from [4] or [8] (p. 3, footnote 2).
- 26% and 33% being estimates (pp. 6, 8).
- In the Notes criterion bullet: the p. 10 conclusion, the per-feature figures (1%/2%, 3%, 26%/15%, 46%) and the rejected variable-size windows (p. 4).
- In the follow-up bullet: the Smalltalk version of the compiler (p. 2), "activation frames are full-fledged Smalltalk objects" with its cause in the language (pp. 7–8), and the authors also being the designers (p. 11).

**Differs (1):** the follow-up bullet (SQ16) says bytecodes are "the semantic definition of the language" (p. 2). The source says "the virtual machine is the semantic definition of the language."

**Fix (in P261.md, `## Notes`, follow-up bullet):**
`the paper says bytecodes are "the semantic definition of the language" and the compiler has a Smalltalk version (p. 2)` → `the paper says "the virtual machine is the semantic definition of the language" and the compiler has a Smalltalk version (p. 2)`

**Not a citation, but noticed (yours to decide):**
- The follow-up bullet lists `by` among the changed frontmatter fields, but the diff shows `by: reader` unchanged; only `status` and `inputs` changed. You could either drop `by` from that list in P261.md (recommended, since it matches the diff) or leave it as is.
- The record says limits on optimisation are "attributed to the language and its bytecodes". The paper also names a third, practical cause: the team's conservative aim of getting a working image, putting "Correctness ... over efficiency" (p. 8). The record quotes the "pragmatic considerations" sentence, so I marked it found and gave no fix.

######## P11
## Suggested fixes
The four fixes of the first check were applied at gate 3c. These are for the follow-up pass only (exact old text → new text in `P11.md`).

1. **Object-table accesses per bytecode (Attributed causes, object-table row).** `accesses the object table 12 times per bytecode [UnP83]"` → `accesses the object table 1.2 times per bytecode [UnP83]"`
2. **Static code cost (Attributed causes, object-table row).** `Static code cost of an object table: "only 2%" of the image (Table 5.14, p. 105).` → `Static code cost of an object table: it "would add only 2% to the size of the system" (p. 105; Table 5.14 gives 2.25% of a 1,500 kB image).`
3. **Compilation value is estimated (Notes, follow-up bullet).** `and the measured value of compiling to a low-level instruction set (pp. 34–35, 68)` → `and the estimated value of compiling to a low-level instruction set ("an approximate doubling in speed", p. 35; Table 4.4's 100% is a "Rough estimate based on discussion with L. P. Deutsch", p. 68)`
######## P15
## Suggested fixes
The earlier fixes (1–3: the sources sentence, "encouraged", and the Common Lisp portability goal) were applied at gate 3c. The fixes below are for claims from the follow-up pass only.

1. **Notes, follow-up bullet, the page range of section 2.8 (differs).** Section 2.8 runs to p. 19.
   - before: `with a second pass of section 2.8 (pp. 16–18)`
   - after: `with a second pass of section 2.8 (pp. 16–19)`
######## P21
## Suggested fixes

The five fixes from the first check were applied at gate 3c. Fixes for the follow-up pass only:

1. Many-core scaling, page of the programmer's view (ref. [11] title is on p. 181):
   `the programmer's view is deferred to [11] (p. 176).` → `the programmer's view is deferred to [11] (cited p. 176; "Programmer's view" in its title, p. 181).`
   and in the same row's page column:
   `| 173–174, 176–177, 179–180 |` → `| 173–174, 176–177, 179–181 |`
######## P46
## Suggested fixes

The ten fixes of the first check were applied at gate 3c and are not repeated. The fix below covers the follow-up pass only.

1. Notes, follow-up bullet, page of "the mandatory part":
   `SQ15 met: the paper argues which memory functions stay in "the mandatory part" and which go to "coexisting alternative memory servers", and what the in-kernel policy gave up (pp. 74–76).`
   →
   `SQ15 met: the paper argues which memory functions stay in the kernel, "mandatory to all other levels" (p. 76), and which go to "coexisting alternative memory servers", and what the in-kernel policy gave up (pp. 74–76).`
######## P48
## Suggested fixes
The four fixes from the first check were applied at gate 3c. The follow-up pass has no claim marked differs or not found, so there is no fix to the paper citations.

One bookkeeping point outside the citations, for the gate (no edit to a paper claim): the *Follow-up pass* bullet lists `by: reader` among the changed frontmatter fields, but the diff shows `by: reader` unchanged (only `status` and `inputs` changed). If the gate wants the bullet exact:
   ``frontmatter (`status: proposed`, `by: reader`, SQ8–SQ19 added to `inputs`)`` → ``frontmatter (`status: proposed`, SQ8–SQ19 added to `inputs`)``
######## P49
## Suggested fixes
The three earlier fixes (Context page, Self-definition, Interposition line counts) were applied at gate 3c and are no longer listed. Fixes below are for the follow-up-pass claims only; old text is exact text in `P49.md`.

1. *Reference* row (Extracted fields), Page column omits p.45, where the SQ17 range starts:
   `| 44, 46, 47, 50, 51 |` → `| 44, 45, 46, 47, 50, 51 |`

######## P66

The earlier fixes (Context, J–Machine; Q3; Q6) were applied at gate 3c. The fixes below cover only the claims of the follow-up pass. Each one is in `P66.md`, in the *Notes* section.
